terms.title: Terms of Use
terms.intro: These terms explain the deal between you and nextED when you use IELTS AI by nextED ("the app"). Please read them — by creating an account or using the app you agree to them.

sections.heading: 1. Who we are
body: IELTS AI is an IELTS Academic preparation app made by nextED, a company based in Bangladesh. When these terms say "we" or "us", they mean nextED.

sections.heading: 2. Not the official IELTS test
body: IELTS is a registered trademark of the British Council, IDP: IELTS Australia and Cambridge University Press & Assessment. IELTS AI is independent: we are not affiliated with, endorsed by or approved by any of them.

Our practice tests are written by us to match the format of the real exam. The bands we give are estimates to guide your study — they are not official results and cannot be used for visa, university or job applications.

sections.heading: 3. Your account
body: You sign up with a Bangladeshi mobile number and a password. Keep your password private: you are responsible for what happens on your account.
Give us accurate details and one account per person. If you are under 18, please use the app with a parent's or guardian's permission.

sections.heading: 4. Using the app fairly
body: You may use the app for your own IELTS preparation. Please don't:
bullets: copy, sell or republish our tests, lessons, sample answers or audio
upload content that is offensive, unlawful or not your own work
try to break, overload or reverse-engineer the app or its AI features
share your account or use someone else's

sections.heading: 5. AI scoring and feedback
body: Your essays and speaking recordings are scored by artificial intelligence (AI). AI can make mistakes, so treat its bands and comments as helpful guidance, not a guarantee of your exam result.
When there is no internet connection some practice is scored offline with a simpler demo model; the app tells you when this happens.

sections.heading: 6. Your content
body: The essays, answers and recordings you create stay yours. You give us permission to store and process them only so we can score them, show you feedback and keep your progress history.

sections.heading: 7. Plans and payment
body: Some features may need a paid plan. Prices and what each plan includes are shown in the app before you pay. We will never charge you without your clear confirmation.

sections.heading: 8. Closing your account
body: You can stop using the app at any time and ask us to delete your account (see the Privacy Policy). We may suspend an account that breaks these terms, after warning you where we reasonably can.

sections.heading: 9. Our responsibility
body: We work hard to keep the app accurate and available, but we provide it "as is". We are not responsible for your official exam result or for losses caused by events outside our reasonable control. Nothing in these terms removes rights you have under the laws of Bangladesh.

sections.heading: 10. Changes and contact
body: If we change these terms we will update the date above and tell you in the app for important changes. These terms are governed by the laws of Bangladesh.
Questions? Email us at support@nexted.app.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.intro: This policy explains what information IELTS AI by nextED collects, why, and the choices you have. In short: we use your data to help you prepare for IELTS, and we never sell it.

sections.heading: 1. What we collect
body: We only collect what the app needs:
bullets: Account details: your name, mobile number and password (stored securely), plus your target band and exam date if you add them
Practice data: your answers, essays, scores, study time, saved words and schedule
Speaking recordings: the audio you record in speaking practice and mock tests
Profile photo, if you choose to add one
Basic technical data such as app version and error reports, so we can fix problems

sections.heading: 2. How we use it
body: We use your information to run your account, score your practice, give feedback, show your progress and study plan, send reminders you have switched on, and improve the app.
We do not use your essays or recordings for advertising.

sections.heading: 3. AI providers
body: To score writing and speaking, your essay text or recording is sent securely to trusted AI service providers who process it on our behalf. They may only use it to provide that service to us, not for their own purposes.

sections.heading: 4. Where your data is stored
body: Your speaking recordings and practice history are stored in secure cloud storage. Some of these providers may keep data on servers outside Bangladesh; we choose providers that protect it with industry-standard security.

sections.heading: 5. We don't sell your data
body: We never sell or rent your personal information. We only share it with the service providers that help us run the app (such as cloud hosting, SMS for verification codes and AI scoring), or when the law requires it.

sections.heading: 6. How long we keep it
body: We keep your data while your account is open so you can see your history. If you delete your account we remove your personal data and recordings within 30 days, except anything we must keep by law.

sections.heading: 7. Your choices and rights
body: You can:
bullets: see and edit your profile in the app
reset your progress from Profile › App settings
remove your profile photo at any time
ask for a copy of your data
ask us to delete your account and recordings: email support@nexted.app and include your registered mobile number

sections.heading: 8. Security
body: We protect your information with encryption in transit, access controls and regular reviews. No system is perfectly secure, so please use a strong password and keep it private.

sections.heading: 9. Young students
body: IELTS AI is designed for students preparing for IELTS Academic. If you are under 18, please use the app with a parent's or guardian's permission.

sections.heading: 10. Changes and contact
body: If we change this policy we will update the date above and let you know in the app about important changes.
Questions or requests about your data? Email support@nexted.app.

lessons.title: Paraphrase spotting
lessons.keyIdea: IELTS rarely repeats the passage word for word. Questions **paraphrase** it — “rose sharply” becomes “increased dramatically”. Match the **meaning**, not the words.

exercises.quote: “The museum’s visitor numbers doubled within two years of the new wing opening.”
exercises.question: Which statement has the same meaning?

options.text: The new wing took two years to build
Twice as many people visited soon after the wing opened
The museum opened two new wings

exercises.quote: “Few residents were aware that the scheme existed.”
exercises.question: Which is the best paraphrase?

options.text: Most residents did not know about the scheme

exercises.quote: “The prototype failed to perform well in cold conditions.”
exercises.question: Which paraphrase is correct?

options.text: The prototype worked best in winter
Low temperatures reduced the prototype’s performance

lessons.title: Skimming vs scanning
lessons.keyIdea: **Skim** for the main idea of each paragraph — first and last sentences. **Scan** for a specific detail — names, numbers, dates — without reading every word.

exercises.quote: “Community projects encourage residents to plant lavender, clover and fruit trees on balconies and in empty lots.”
exercises.question: Where are residents encouraged to plant?

options.text: On balconies and in empty lots

exercises.quote: “Bees were first kept on London rooftops in the 1990s, but numbers only rose sharply after 2008.”
exercises.question: When did rooftop hive numbers rise sharply?

exercises.quote: “Supporters argue that cities offer bees a surprising advantage.”
exercises.question: Skim the sentence. What is the main idea?

options.text: Cities can be good places for bees

lessons.title: False or Not Given?
lessons.keyIdea: Choose **False** only when the passage says the **opposite**. If the passage simply does not tell you, the answer is **Not Given** — never use your own knowledge.

exercises.quote: “The bridge was completed in 1932, two years later than planned.”
exercises.question: Statement: The bridge opened on schedule.
Statement: The farmers were paid for taking part.

exercises.quote: “Unlike earlier models, the new engine runs on hydrogen alone.”
exercises.question: Statement: Earlier models did not run on hydrogen alone.

lessons.title: Reference words
lessons.keyIdea: Words like **this**, **these**, **it** and **such** point back to an earlier idea. Work out what they refer to and you can follow the argument from sentence to sentence.

exercises.quote: “Engineers added a second cooling fan. This reduced the temperature by 12 degrees.”
exercises.question: What does “This” refer to?

exercises.quote: “Bamboo grows rapidly and needs little water. These qualities make it attractive to builders.”
exercises.question: What are “these qualities”?

options.text: Fast growth and low water needs

exercises.quote: “Early maps often exaggerated coastlines. Such errors misled sailors for centuries.”
exercises.question: What does “Such errors” refer to?

blocks.note: Approximate: the official conversion shifts slightly from test to test. The app uses this table for your practice scores.

blocks.title: General Training: raw score to band
blocks.note: General Training needs more correct answers for the same band because its texts are easier.

blocks.title: What Reading tests
items: Skimming for the general meaning and structure
Recognising the writer's opinions, attitudes and claims

blocks.title: How answers are marked
items: No penalty for wrong answers, so never leave a blank.
There is no extra time to transfer answers: write them on the answer sheet as you go.
Academic texts come from books, journals, magazines and newspapers, written for a non-specialist reader.

skills.name: Writing
skills.intro: An examiner marks each task on four criteria, each worth 25% of that task's band. Task 2 counts twice as much as Task 1.

blocks.title: How the Writing band is made
blocks.note: Writing band = (Task 1 + 2 × Task 2) ÷ 3, rounded to the nearest half band. Example: Task 1 = 6.0 and Task 2 = 7.0 → (6 + 14) ÷ 3 = 6.67 → 6.5.

blocks.title: Criteria
blocks.subtitle: Task Achievement is used for Task 1 and Task Response for Task 2. The other three apply to both tasks.

criteria.name: Task Achievement
focus: Answers exactly what the task asks
Picks out the key features instead of listing every number
Gives a clear overview of the main trends, differences or stages
Supports the key features with accurate data
At least 150 words

levels.text: Fully meets the task. A clear, well-chosen overview, with the key features fully presented and illustrated.
Covers every requirement well. Key features are clearly highlighted and well supported, with a clear overview.
Covers the requirements. A clear overview of the main trends or differences; key features are highlighted but could be developed more.
Addresses the task. An overview is attempted, but data may be listed mechanically, and some details are inaccurate or irrelevant.
Only partly covers the task. No clear overview, details recounted mechanically, and key features not covered well; data may be missing.
Attempts the task but misses or confuses the key features; much of the content is irrelevant or inaccurate.

criteria.name: Task Response
focus: Answers every part of the question
Keeps a clear position from start to finish
Develops ideas: idea → explanation → example
Stays relevant to the question
At least 250 words

levels.text: Fully answers every part of the question with a fully developed position and relevant, well-supported ideas.
Answers every part well. Ideas are relevant, extended and supported, with only occasional gaps.
Answers every part. A clear position throughout; main ideas are extended and supported, though some may over-generalise.
Answers every part, some more fully than others. The position is relevant, but some ideas are underdeveloped or the conclusion is unclear.
Answers the task only partly. The position is unclear at times; ideas are limited, underdeveloped or partly irrelevant.
Responds only minimally or goes off the point. The position is unclear and ideas are few, repetitive or unsupported.

criteria.name: Coherence & Cohesion
focus: Ideas in a logical order with clear progression
One clear main idea per paragraph
Linking words used naturally, not just often
Clear referencing (this, these, the former, the latter)

levels.text: Cohesion is so natural it attracts no attention; paragraphing is skilful.
Ideas are sequenced logically, cohesion is well managed, and paragraphing is used well.
Logical organisation and clear progression; a range of linking devices, with some under- or over-use; each paragraph has a clear central topic.
Coherent overall with clear progression, but linking can be mechanical or faulty, and referencing is not always clear.
Some organisation but no overall progression; linking words are limited, inaccurate or overused; paragraphing may be inadequate.
Ideas are not arranged coherently; basic linking words are repetitive or wrong, and there are no clear paragraphs.

criteria.name: Lexical Resource
focus: Range: enough words to express ideas precisely
Accuracy of word choice and spelling
Natural collocations (a sharp rise, not a powerful rise)
Correct word formation (noun, verb, adjective, adverb)
Style suited to formal writing

levels.text: A wide range of vocabulary used naturally and precisely; only very rare slips.
A wide range used fluently and flexibly; less common words used skilfully, with rare errors in spelling or word choice.
Enough range for some flexibility and precision; less common words used with awareness of style and collocation; occasional errors.
An adequate range for the task; less common words attempted with some inaccuracy; spelling or word-formation errors that do not block meaning.
A limited range that is only just adequate; noticeable spelling and word-formation errors may make reading harder.
Only basic vocabulary, often repetitive or inappropriate; poor control of spelling and word formation strains the reader.

criteria.name: Grammatical Range & Accuracy
focus: Variety: simple, compound and complex sentences
Accuracy: articles, agreement, tenses, prepositions, plurals
Correct punctuation and sentence boundaries
Complex grammar used with control, not just attempted

levels.text: A wide range of structures used flexibly and accurately; only rare minor slips.
A wide range of structures; most sentences are error-free, with only very occasional mistakes.
A variety of complex structures; frequent error-free sentences and good control of grammar and punctuation, with a few errors.
A mix of simple and complex sentences; some grammar and punctuation errors, but they rarely reduce communication.
A limited range; complex sentences are attempted but less accurate than simple ones; frequent errors can cause some difficulty.
A very limited range with few subordinate clauses; errors dominate and punctuation is often faulty.

blocks.title: Good to know
items: Writing under the word limit lowers your Task Achievement / Task Response band.
Memorised "advanced" words do not raise your band if they are used unnaturally.
Complex grammar only helps when it is accurate.

skills.name: Speaking
skills.intro: A face-to-face interview with an examiner, marked on four equally weighted criteria across all three parts. Your band is the average of the four.

items.label: Part 1
items.title: Introduction and interview · 4–5 min
items.text: Questions about familiar topics: home, work or studies, hobbies, daily life.

items.label: Part 2
items.title: Long turn · 3–4 min
items.text: A cue card with a topic. One minute to prepare, then speak for 1–2 minutes; the examiner may ask one or two follow-up questions.

items.label: Part 3
items.title: Discussion · 4–5 min
items.text: More abstract questions linked to Part 2: explain, compare, speculate and give reasons.

criteria.name: Fluency & Coherence
focus: Speaks at length without long pauses
Hesitation is to find ideas, not words
Little repetition or self-correction
Answers are organised and extended
Connects ideas with a range of linking words

levels.text: Speaks fluently with only rare repetition or self-correction; any hesitation is about ideas, not language; topics fully developed.
Speaks fluently with only occasional repetition or self-correction; develops topics coherently and appropriately.
Speaks at length without noticeable effort or loss of coherence; some language-related hesitation; uses linking words flexibly.
Willing to speak at length, but may lose coherence through repetition, self-correction or hesitation; linking words not always appropriate.
Usually keeps going, but relies on repetition, self-correction or slow speech; overuses some linking words; complex ideas cause problems.
Cannot answer without noticeable pauses; speaks slowly with frequent repetition; only simple links between basic sentences.

criteria.name: Lexical Resource
focus: Range of vocabulary across familiar and unfamiliar topics
Precise word choice
Natural idiomatic language and collocations
Paraphrases when the exact word is missing

levels.text: Full flexibility and precision on every topic; idiomatic language used naturally and accurately.
A wide range used readily and flexibly; less common and idiomatic words used skilfully, with occasional slips; paraphrases well.
Uses vocabulary flexibly across a variety of topics; some less common and idiomatic words, with some poor choices; paraphrases well.
A range wide enough to talk at length and make meaning clear despite some wrong choices; generally paraphrases successfully.
Manages familiar and unfamiliar topics but with little flexibility; paraphrasing works only some of the time.
Talks about familiar topics but only conveys basic meaning on unfamiliar ones; frequent wrong words; rarely paraphrases.

criteria.name: Grammatical Range & Accuracy
focus: Range: simple, complex, conditional, passive and relative structures
Accuracy while speaking spontaneously
How often errors happen and whether they confuse the listener

levels.text: A full range of structures used naturally; consistently accurate apart from the slips native speakers make.
A wide range of structures used flexibly; most sentences are error-free, with only occasional mistakes.
A range of complex structures with some flexibility; frequent error-free sentences, though some mistakes remain.
A mix of simple and complex structures with limited flexibility; frequent mistakes in complex sentences, which rarely cause confusion.
Basic sentences are fairly accurate; complex structures are limited, usually contain errors and may cause problems.
Mostly basic sentences, with rare subordinate clauses; errors are frequent and may cause misunderstanding.

criteria.name: Pronunciation
focus: Clear individual sounds
Correct word and sentence stress
Natural rhythm, intonation and connected speech
How easily the listener understands you (accent itself is not marked down)

levels.text: A full range of pronunciation features used precisely; effortless to understand throughout; accent has no effect.
A wide range of features used flexibly with only occasional lapses; easy to understand throughout; accent has minimal effect.
All the strengths of band 6 and some, but not all, of band 8.
A range of features with mixed control; generally understood throughout, though some words or sounds are mispronounced.
All the strengths of band 4 and some, but not all, of band 6.
A limited range of features with frequent lapses; mispronunciations are common and make the listener work hard.

blocks.title: Good to know
items: You do not need a British, American or Australian accent: being easy to understand is what counts.
Fluency is not speed. Natural pauses to think are fine; constant stops to find words are not.
Short answers limit your band: extend each answer with a reason or example.

skills.name: Overall
skills.intro: Each skill gets a band from 0 to 9 (half bands possible). Your overall band is the average of the four, rounded.

blocks.title: Rounding the average
rows: Up to the next whole band

items.name: Expert
items.text: Full command of English: appropriate, accurate and fluent, with complete understanding.

items.name: Very good
items.text: Full command with only occasional unsystematic errors; handles complex argument well.

items.name: Good
items.text: Operational command with occasional errors and misunderstandings in some situations.

items.name: Competent
items.text: Generally effective command despite some errors and misunderstandings.

items.name: Modest
items.text: Partial command; copes with overall meaning in most situations but makes many mistakes.

items.name: Limited
items.text: Basic competence in familiar situations; frequent problems with understanding and expression.

items.name: Extremely limited
items.text: Conveys and understands only general meaning in very familiar situations.

items.name: Intermittent
items.text: Great difficulty understanding spoken and written English.

items.name: Non-user
items.text: No ability to use the language beyond a few isolated words.

blocks.title: Two kinds of scoring
items: Listening and Reading: counted. Correct answers → raw score → band.
Writing and Speaking: judged. An examiner rates four criteria against the band descriptors.
Bands are not percentages: band 7 does not mean 70% correct.

tips.title: Understanding IELTS Listening
tips.body:
Four parts, forty questions, and every recording plays once. Answers come in the same order as the audio and get harder from Part 1 to Part 4. On the computer test you type as you listen, with about two minutes to check at the end.

**Why it matters:** You cannot outsmart a test you do not understand. High scorers walk in knowing the shape of every part, when each answer arrives, and where the traps sit.
**The test at a glance**
• **4 parts, 40 questions**, with 10 questions in each part.
• **About 30 minutes of audio**, and every recording plays **once only**.
• **Answers follow the audio order.** The answer to Q3 is always spoken before Q4.
• **Difficulty climbs:** Part 1 is the gentlest, Part 4 the hardest.
**The four parts**
• **Part 1: two people, everyday.** A booking or enquiry full of names, dates, prices and addresses. The cheapest marks in the exam, so aim for all ten.
• **Part 2: one speaker, everyday.** A talk about a place, event or facility. The speaker's signposting (first, next, on your left) is your map.
• **Part 3: up to four speakers, education.** Students and a tutor discussing work. Opinions change mid-sentence and distractors are everywhere.
• **Part 4: one speaker, academic.** A lecture with dense information and few pauses. Concentration is the whole game.
**Timing on the computer test**
• There is **no ten-minute transfer time**. Older books that still teach it are out of date.
• **Type each answer straight into the box** the moment you hear it.
• You get **about two minutes at the end** to review. That is for slips, not for rebuilding answers from memory.
• You can **highlight and make notes on screen** during the audio, so use them.
**How the answers reach you**
• Before each part, a short pause lets you read the questions. **This pause is gold.**
• Answers arrive in natural speech, **almost never in the question's words**. Same meaning, different clothes.
• **Twelve question types** recur: six completion types (form, note, table, flow-chart, summary, sentence), plus multiple choice, multiple-answer, matching, map labelling, diagram labelling and short answer.
**Distractors: a first look**
• A distractor is **planted information** that pulls you towards a wrong answer. It is designed, not accidental.
• **The correction:** "Room 214, sorry, room 240." The word sorry is the signal.
• **The choice:** "Wednesday, but Thursday works better." Both are said; only one is chosen.
**How your score works**
• **One mark per correct answer**, and **no penalty** for wrong answers. Never leave a blank.
• **30 to 31 correct is about Band 7**, so you can miss nine or ten and still get there.
• **35 to 36 is about Band 8**, and 39 to 40 is Band 9.
• One lost answer is never a disaster. Chasing it in panic costs far more.
**Tutor insider tip**
Practise on a screen, not on paper. The most common test-day shock is discovering there is no transfer time and every answer must go straight into the box. Train the way you will play.

tips.title: The Listening Mindset
tips.body:
Listening is not a comprehension test; it is a live hunt. Read ahead in every pause, predict what each gap needs, and when you miss an answer, let it go instantly so it does not cost you the next one.

**Why it matters:** Two students with the same English can score two full bands apart. The difference is almost never in the ears. It is in the head.
**The reframe**
• Listening is **a live hunt**, not a comprehension exercise. You catch specific facts as they fly past, once, while reading, predicting and recovering at the same time.
• The audio moves **one way only** and never comes back.
**Your only real weapon: reading ahead**
• You cannot control the recording. You fully control **what you do in the pauses**.
• Reading ahead means knowing what each question asks, so that **a bell rings** when the answer arrives.
• A candidate who read ahead is **waiting** for the answer. One who did not is **reacting**, always half a second late.
**Predict the shape, not the answer**
• Before the audio, decide what each gap needs: **a number, a name, a plural noun, a time or a date**.
• Prediction turns thirty minutes of sound into **a series of small, targeted catches**.
**Two listening modes**
• **Specific information (narrow ear):** one fact such as a price, a platform number or a surname. Form, note and table completion live here.
• **Meaning (wide ear):** attitude, agreement, direction. Multiple choice, matching and most of Parts 3 and 4 live here.
• The question type tells you **which mode to switch on** before the audio starts.
**Following the talk**
• In **Parts 2 and 4**, use the speaker's structure words (firstly, however, the main reason) as a handrail.
• In **Part 3**, also track **who is speaking** and what each person thinks.
**Attention is a budget**
• Thirty minutes of listening is tiring, and focus dips, especially in Part 4.
• **Sharpen as each answer approaches**, relax slightly once it is safely captured, then sharpen again.
**The recovery reflex**
• Every high scorer misses answers. The disaster is **chasing the miss**, because the next answer arrives while you are looking back.
• Build the **clean reset**: recognise the miss, let it go, rejoin at the next question.
• Panic is attention pointed at fear. The cure is **an immediate task**: eyes to the next question, ear hunting the next target.
**Three heads, one moment**
Gap: member rate. Audio: "It's normally forty pounds a night, but for members it comes down to thirty-two."
• **Beginner:** writes 40, relaxes, and misses the change.
• **Experienced:** hears "but", writes 32, but a beat late.
• **Expert:** saw "member" in the gap, so "for members" rang the bell. Never tempted by 40 at all.
The gap between them is not English. **It is preparation and expectation.**
**Tutor insider tip**
One missed answer should never cost you the next three. The moment you feel yourself reaching back for a lost answer, drop it and move your eyes to the next question.

tips.title: Question Prediction
tips.body:
Before the audio starts, ask of every gap: what kind of answer am I about to hear? A number, a name, a verb, a plural noun? That one question sets a filter that lets you catch one word out of two hundred.

**Why it matters:** Prediction is the habit that most separates a Band 8 candidate from a Band 6 one. The beginner reads a question and waits. The expert reads it and knows what is coming.
**The one question**
• Ask of every gap: **"What kind of answer am I about to hear?"**
• That question sets **a filter** in your mind, so the right word stands out from the flood.
**Predict on two layers**
• **Layer 1, grammar:** is the missing word a noun, verb, adjective or number?
• "open until ____" needs **a time**
• "must not ____ inside" needs **a verb**
• "surprisingly ____" needs **an adjective**
• "bring your own ____" needs **a countable noun**
• **Layer 2, information type:** name, place, measurement, date, price, object or role.
**What your ear waits for**
• **A number:** digits, quantities, prices
• **A date:** days, months, four-digit years
• **A time:** clock times, "quarter past", "half past"
• **A name:** often spelled out, letter by letter
• **A measurement:** metres, kilos, minutes, percentages
• **A role:** manager, guide, receptionist, professor
**Read around the gap**
• Read the words **after** the gap too. They often fix the grammar better than the words before.
• "The museum's ____ collection" only becomes predictable once you see **collection**.
**Singular or plural**
• "there is a ____" forces **singular**; "guests are given two ____" forces **plural**.
• If what you catch does not match what you predicted, treat it as **an alarm** that you misheard.
**Respect the word limit**
• "ONE WORD ONLY" or "NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER" is a rule, not advice.
• Three words where two are allowed is **wrong**, even if the meaning is perfect.
• **Hyphenated words count as one word** (part-time, check-in). **Figures count as a number**, not a word.
**Worked example**
Notes: Name, Number of nights, Room type ____ room, Extra charge for ____.
• Name: **a surname, probably spelled**
• Nights: **a small number**
• Room type: **a short adjective** (single, double, deluxe)
• Extra charge: **a noun** (breakfast, parking, wifi)
Four nets set in fifteen seconds. **Each answer drops into the net waiting for it.**
**Tutor insider tip**
If you finish predicting before the audio starts, do not sit idle. Read ahead into the next set. The pauses are never long enough for a slow reader.

tips.title: Keywords
tips.body:
Underlining everything is underlining nothing. Mark only the few words that will actually locate the answer. Names, numbers and dates are your best anchors, because the exam can reword almost anything except them.

**Why it matters:** Struggling candidates underline almost every word. Keyword skill is choosing the few words that will actually find the answer, and ignoring the rest.
**Not all words are equal**
• **Strong keywords** carry the specific meaning: unusual nouns, specific verbs, the topic.
• **Weak keywords** carry little information: the, a, some, thing, people.
• **Unique keywords** appear nowhere else: a proper name, a number, a technical term. **The most valuable of all.**
• **Generic keywords** are broad and locate poorly: problem, change, area.
• **Concept keywords** carry an idea and **warn you a paraphrase is coming**.
**The anchor principle**
• **Names, numbers and dates are almost never paraphrased.** Content words almost always are.
• The exam can turn "cheap" into "won't break the bank", but **1985 can only ever be 1985**.
**Your priority order**
• **Unique anchors** (names, numbers, dates, technical terms): mark these first.
• **Strong content words:** mark them, but expect them to be reworded.
• **Concept words:** note them mentally as a paraphrase warning.
• **Weak and generic words:** ignore them.
**Worked example**
"In 1996, the company moved its headquarters to ____."
• Best keyword: **1996**.
• When you hear "in ninety-six", you know **the answer is arriving now**.
• Even if "moved its headquarters" becomes "relocated its main offices", the anchor holds.
**How to mark fast**
• **One keyword per question** is usually enough.
• **Circle the anchor**, then relax about the rest of the sentence.
• For content words, spend **two seconds** thinking how else they might be said.
**Quick practice**
Pick the one word you would rely on:
• "How much does the annual pass cost?" → **cost** (strong, expect "price")
• "In 2010, the factory switched to solar power." → **2010** (anchor)
• "Passengers should report to Professor Nolan." → **Nolan** (anchor)
**Traps to watch**
• **Over-marking:** ten underlines means your eye has nowhere to land.
• **Waiting for the exact word:** content words will be reworded, so listen for meaning.
• **Ignoring the anchor:** a name or number in the question is the exam handing you a word it cannot disguise.
**Tutor insider tip**
When a question contains a number or a name, that is usually your single best keyword. Circle it and relax about the rest.

tips.title: Paraphrase Recognition
tips.body:
The question and the audio say the same thing in different words. The exam tests whether you recognise meaning, not whether you hear a matching word. Pre-load two or three alternatives for each keyword before you listen.

**Why it matters:** Paraphrase is the mechanism the whole test runs on. Understand it and the exam stops feeling like a trap and starts feeling like a translation you can do.
**The principle**
• **Same meaning, different words.** The audio will almost never repeat the question's wording.
• The test checks **recognition of meaning**, not matching of sounds.
**Seven forms paraphrase takes**
• **Synonym:** cost becomes price, fee, charge.
• **Word-class change:** "the decision to close" becomes "they decided to close".
• **Active/passive swap:** "the council built the bridge" becomes "the bridge was built by the council".
• **Expression:** "cheap" becomes "won't break the bank".
• **Indirect wording:** the answer is implied, not stated.
• **Numerical:** 50% becomes "half"; doubled becomes "twice as many".
• **Conceptual:** the whole idea is rebuilt with no shared words at all.
**Predict the paraphrase**
• Take your strong keyword and ask: **"If they don't say this word, how else might they say it?"**
• Spend **two seconds** per keyword generating alternatives.
• This is **the highest-value drill in the module**, where prediction and paraphrase meet.
**A quick bank**
• **buy:** purchase, pick up, pay for
• **dangerous:** risky, unsafe, hazardous
• **increase:** rise, go up, climb
• **nearby:** close by, within walking distance
• **important:** crucial, vital, key, essential
• **children:** kids, youngsters, the young
**Three heads, one moment**
Question: "The main disadvantage of the site was its ____."
Audio: "The one real drawback with the location was how far it sat from the station."
• **Beginner:** waits for "disadvantage", never hears it, and misses the sentence.
• **Experienced:** catches "drawback" as a match, but a beat late.
• **Expert:** had pre-loaded disadvantage = drawback, downside, problem. Caught **distance from the station** cleanly.
The expert did not hear better. **They expected better.**
**What changes and what doesn't**
• **Content words:** listen for their **meaning**.
• **Names, numbers, dates:** listen for their **sound**.
**Tutor insider tip**
The words most likely to be paraphrased are the content words in the question. The words least likely to change are names, numbers and dates.

tips.title: Form Completion
tips.body:
Form completion is usually the first task in Part 1: a form with labelled fields such as Name, Date and Phone. Predict every field, wait for spelled letters, and expect at least one number to be corrected.

**Why it matters:** These are the cheapest marks in the whole exam and usually the first thing you meet. Losing them to a spelling slip or a correction is one of the most expensive mistakes you can make.
**Recognise it**
• A form with **labelled fields**: Name, Address, Date, Phone, Reference.
• **Almost always Part 1**, often the very first questions.
**What it tests**
• Catching **concrete personal and factual details** in real speech.
• Listening for specific information at its purest: **narrow ear on**.
**Before the audio**
• Read **every field label** and turn each into a prediction.
• Note **the word limit** before anything else.
• Mark which fields are likely **spelled** (names, streets) and which are **numbers** (phone, postcode, price).
**During the audio**
• Answers come **in order, one field at a time**.
• The person filling in the form often **repeats the detail back**, giving you a second chance to confirm.
• **Write fast and rough**, and keep one eye on the next field.
**Traps to watch**
• **Corrections** on numbers: "three, no sorry, four nights".
• **Spelled names** with letters that sound alike: m/n, b/p, and the British "e".
• **Postcodes** that mix letters and digits.
• **Numbers stated, then adjusted** a sentence later.
**Beginner vs expert**
• **Beginner:** writes the first thing heard, relaxes, misses the correction, or panics over spelling and loses the next field.
• **Expert:** predicts every field, writes rough, and never lets one field cost the next.
**Worked example**
Fields: Surname ____, Arrival date ____, Number of nights ____.
Audio: "It's Hendricks, H-E-N-D-R-I-C-K-S... The fourteenth of March... Three, no sorry, four nights."
• **Hendricks**, taken from the letters, not the sound
• **14 March**
• **four**, not three, caught by "no sorry"
**Final check**
• Is every name **spelled exactly** as it was spelled out?
• Did any number have **a correction** after it?
• Is each answer **within the word limit**?
**Tutor insider tip**
In Part 1, expect names and reference codes to be spelled out. Do not guess the spelling from the sound; wait for the letters and write them as they come.

tips.title: Note Completion
tips.body:
Note completion gives you a skeleton of notes with gaps, laid out the way someone would jot down a talk. Read the headings first: they are your map, and the speaker will move through them in order.

**Why it matters:** Common in Parts 2 and 4, note completion rewards candidates who follow a talk's structure. Lose your place under one heading and several answers can go at once.
**Recognise it**
• A **title**, then **headings and bullet points** with gaps.
• Laid out like **someone's notes on a talk**. Common in **Parts 2 and 4**.
**What it tests**
• Following **the structure of a talk**.
• Pulling out **key details** as the speaker moves from point to point.
**Before the audio**
• Read **the headings first**. They show the shape of the talk and where you are at any moment.
• Then read **the gaps** and predict each one's shape.
• Note **the word limit**.
**During the audio**
• The speaker's **signposting lines up with your headings**. When they change topic, you move too.
• Answers come **in order, under each heading in turn**.
• Write **only the word that fits** the note, not everything the speaker says.
**Traps to watch**
• **Extra true detail** that fits the topic but not the specific note.
• **Paraphrase** between the heading word and the audio.
• **Losing your place** when a speaker lingers on one point.
**Beginner vs expert**
• **Beginner:** reads the notes as continuous prose and gets lost.
• **Expert:** uses headings as anchors, predicts the gap, and writes the one word that fits.
**Worked example**
Notes: The town museum. Opened: originally a ____. Best-known exhibit: a Roman ____.
Audio: "The building started life as a flour mill before becoming a museum in the 1970s. Its most famous piece is a beautifully preserved Roman helmet."
• "Started life as" paraphrases **originally**. Answer: **flour mill**.
• "Most famous piece" paraphrases **best-known exhibit**. Answer: **helmet**.
• "The 1970s" is true detail, but **no gap asks for it**.
**Quick check**
• Did I stay **under the right heading**?
• Does my answer **fit the note grammatically**?
• Am I **within the word limit**?
**Tutor insider tip**
Headings are your map. If you lose your place, look at the next heading, not the next gap, and wait for the speaker's signpost that moves you into it.

tips.title: Table Completion
tips.body:
Table completion asks you to track information across rows and columns at the same time. Read the headers first, keep a mental finger on the current cell, and match each number to its exact row.

**Why it matters:** Tables pack a lot of information into one grid. One slip in tracking the current row can corrupt several answers in a row.
**Recognise it**
• A **grid of rows and columns** with some cells empty.
• Often compares **courses, prices, times or options**.
**What it tests**
• Tracking information along **two dimensions at once**.
• Slotting each detail into **the right cell**.
**Before the audio**
• Read **the row and column headers first**. They are the categories the speaker will move through.
• Predict each empty cell from **its column header**: a price column wants a number, a day column wants a day.
• Note **the word limit**.
**During the audio**
• The table usually fills **left to right, top to bottom**, matching the speaker's order.
• Listen for **header words or their paraphrases** to know which cell is live.
• Keep **a mental finger on the current cell** and move it deliberately.
**Traps to watch**
• **Two rows discussing similar things**, so you jump to the wrong cell.
• **Numbers that belong to a neighbouring cell**.
• **One sentence carrying several cells' worth** of data at once.
**Beginner vs expert**
• **Beginner:** loses track of the row, and one slip ruins several answers.
• **Expert:** re-anchors on the headers and moves cell by cell.
**Worked example**
Pottery / Tuesday / ____ (cost). Drawing / ____ (day) / 40 pounds.
Audio: "Pottery runs on Tuesdays and costs fifty pounds. Drawing is a bit cheaper at forty, and that one's on Thursdays."
• Pottery cost: **50 pounds**
• Drawing day: **Thursday**
• Forty is already printed in the drawing row, so **it cannot be the pottery answer**.
**Quick check**
• Does each answer sit in **the row it was spoken about**?
• Does it match **the type its column needs**?
• Have I used a number that **already appears** elsewhere in the table?
**Tutor insider tip**
In tables, the headers are your safety rail. If you ever feel lost, snap your eyes back to the row and column headers rather than to the gap itself.

tips.title: Flow-chart Completion
tips.body:
A flow-chart shows the stages of a process as boxes joined by arrows. Read the whole chart first so you understand the process, ride the sequence words, and stay alert when the speaker doubles back.

**Why it matters:** Processes are described strictly in order, which makes flow-charts predictable, until the speaker adds or reorders a step and your boxes slide out of line.
**Recognise it**
• **Boxes connected by arrows** showing the stages of a process.
• Some boxes are empty for you to complete.
**What it tests**
• Following **a described process in order**.
• Identifying **each stage or action**.
**Before the audio**
• Read **the whole chart top to bottom** so you understand the process before it is described.
• Decide whether each gap is **an action (verb-led)** or **a thing (noun-led)**.
• Note **the word limit**.
**During the audio**
• Ride the **sequence language**: first, then, next, after that, once this is done, finally.
• Answers come **strictly in the order of the arrows**.
• Count the stages as they pass so you **always know which box is live**.
**Traps to watch**
• **Order-adjusting phrases:** "but before that, you need to..."
• **Extra sub-steps** mentioned that are not boxes on the chart.
• **Paraphrased action words:** "sign" may arrive as "get it approved".
**Beginner vs expert**
• **Beginner:** treats each box in isolation and misses it when the speaker doubles back.
• **Expert:** rides the sequence words and reacts to every "before that".
**Worked example**
Collect form → ____ → Submit to office → ____.
Audio: "First you collect the form. Then you'll need to get it signed by your supervisor before you submit it. After submitting, you simply wait for confirmation by email."
• Box 2: **get it signed**
• Box 4: **wait for confirmation**
• "By your supervisor" is extra detail. Under a short word limit, **leave it out**.
**Quick check**
• Does each answer describe **a stage**, in the right form (verb or noun)?
• Did any "before that" **insert a step** I need to account for?
• Is each answer **within the word limit**?
**Tutor insider tip**
When you hear "before that" or "but first", stop and check which box the new step belongs to. An inserted step can push every later answer one box down.

tips.title: Summary Completion
tips.body:
Summary completion gives a paragraph with gaps that retells part of the recording in different words. Read the whole summary for meaning first. If there is a word box, eliminate options by grammar before meaning.

**Why it matters:** The summary itself is paraphrased, so candidates who hunt for its exact words in the audio hear nothing. This task rewards listening for meaning.
**Recognise it**
• **A paragraph** summarising part of the recording, with several gaps.
• Sometimes filled **from a box of words**, sometimes from the audio.
**What it tests**
• Following **a stretch of talk** and capturing its key content words.
• Coping with **a summary that is itself reworded**.
**Before the audio**
• Read **the whole summary first** to understand its overall meaning.
• Then predict **each gap's part of speech**.
• Expect the surrounding words **not to match** the audio exactly.
**During the audio**
• Listen for **the meaning** of each sentence, then catch the word that completes it.
• Answers usually come **in order** across the summarised section.
**With a word box**
• There are **always more options than gaps**. The extras are traps.
• **Eliminate by grammar first:** a gap after "a" cannot take a plural noun.
• **Then decide by meaning** among what remains.
**Traps to watch**
• **Spare words** built to fit the topic but not the sentence.
• **Exact-word hunting:** waiting for the summary's wording, which never comes.
**Beginner vs expert**
• **Beginner:** tries to match the summary's words to the audio and hears nothing.
• **Expert:** reads for meaning and narrows the options by grammar.
**Worked example**
"The scheme was first introduced to reduce ____ in the city centre, and proved most popular with ____."
Audio: "The initiative began as a way of cutting down on traffic congestion downtown, and interestingly it was the elderly who took it up most enthusiastically."
• "Cutting down on" = **reduce**; "downtown" = **city centre**. Answer: **congestion**.
• "Took it up most enthusiastically" = **most popular with**. Answer: **the elderly**.
**Quick check**
• Does the completed summary **read as good English**?
• Does each answer carry **the audio's meaning**?
• With a box, have I used **each option once at most**, unless told otherwise?
**Tutor insider tip**
When a summary gives you a box of words, count the options against the gaps. The spare words are traps built to fit the topic but not the sentence. Eliminate by grammar before you decide by meaning.

tips.title: Sentence Completion
tips.body:
Sentence completion gives separate sentences, each with a gap to fill from the recording. Treat each sentence as a template: your answer must carry the right meaning and fit the grammar within the word limit.

**Why it matters:** An answer can mean exactly the right thing and still be marked wrong because it doesn't fit the sentence or breaks the word limit.
**Recognise it**
• **A list of separate sentences**, each with one gap.
• Unlike a summary, they **do not form one flowing paragraph**.
**What it tests**
• Catching **specific information**.
• Fitting it **grammatically** into a given sentence frame.
**Before the audio**
• Read each sentence and predict **the gap's part of speech and meaning**.
• The fixed half of the sentence usually holds **the keyword that will be paraphrased**.
• Note **the word limit**.
**During the audio**
• Answers come **in order down the list**.
• Catch the **meaning** first, then trim to the words that fit.
**Traps to watch**
• **Grammatical mismatches:** a phrase that means the right thing but doesn't slot in.
• **Over-length answers** that break the limit.
• **Related detail** that fits the topic but not this sentence.
**Beginner vs expert**
• **Beginner:** writes a whole heard phrase without checking it fits.
• **Expert:** reads the completed sentence back in their head to check it makes sense.
**Worked example**
"The new policy was designed to help ____ find affordable housing."
Audio: "The whole point of the reform was to give first-time buyers a realistic chance of getting onto the property ladder without being priced out."
• "The whole point of the reform" = **the policy was designed to**.
• "Getting onto the property ladder" = **find affordable housing**.
• Answer: **first-time buyers**.
**Try one**
"The material is valued for being lightweight and ____." (ONE WORD)
Audio: "What makes it so useful is that it's both very light and surprisingly durable."
• Answer: **durable**. "Very light" paraphrases lightweight, which is already in the sentence.
**The read-back test**
• Put your answer **into the gap**.
• Read **the whole sentence** silently.
• Does it **make sense and sound correct**?
• Is it **within the limit**?
**Tutor insider tip**
Always read the finished sentence back in your head. If it sounds wrong, the answer is wrong, however clearly you heard it.

tips.title: Multiple Choice
tips.body:
In multiple choice, all three options are usually mentioned in the audio, on purpose. Work out how the options differ before you listen, then wait for the speaker's verdict rather than the first familiar word.

**Why it matters:** Multiple choice feels easy because the answer is printed on the page. It is harder than it looks, because the exam names every option to tempt you.
**Recognise it**
• **A question stem** followed by **three options: A, B, C**.
• Often about **an opinion, a reason or the gist**, not a single fact.
**What it tests**
• **Detailed understanding** of what the speaker actually means.
• Your ability to separate **mention from endorsement**.
**Before the audio**
• Read **the stem and all three options**.
• Work out **how the options differ**. That difference is what you are really listening for.
• Pre-load **paraphrases** for each option's key idea.
**During the audio**
• Expect language linked to **all three options**, by design.
• Treat every option as **"mentioned until endorsed"**.
• Wait for **verdict words**: I think, in the end, what matters most, so we chose, that's why.
**Traps to watch**
• **Two similar options** discussed before one is chosen.
• **An option mentioned, then rejected.**
• **Positive-sounding mentions** of options that are not the final choice.
**Beginner vs expert**
• **Beginner:** picks the option whose words arrive first.
• **Expert:** waits for the verdict and lets the decoys pass.
**Worked example**
"Why did the team change suppliers?" A) price B) quality C) delivery times.
Audio: "The old supplier was actually cheaper, and the quality was fine, but they kept missing deadlines, and that's ultimately why we switched."
• Price and quality: **mentioned, both dismissed**.
• "Kept missing deadlines" paraphrases **delivery times**, confirmed by "that's ultimately why".
• Answer: **C**.
**Try one**
"What does the speaker like most about the new office?" A) the location B) the light C) the space.
Audio: "It's bigger than the old one, which is nice, and the commute's easier now. But honestly, what I love is how bright it is."
• Answer: **B**. "What I love is" is the verdict; size and commute are mild decoys.
**Tutor insider tip**
Mention is not endorsement. Do not tick an option because you heard its words; tick it when the speaker commits to it.

tips.title: Multiple-Answer Questions
tips.body:
Questions that say choose TWO scatter the correct answers among decoys, and some options are named only to be cancelled. Keep every option live, and tick one only when the speaker clearly confirms it.

**Why it matters:** With five options and two answers, three options are traps. The exam loves to name a tempting option and then quietly cancel it.
**Recognise it**
• "Which **TWO** things..." or "Choose **THREE**", with a longer list of options.
• Usually **five to seven options** for two or three answers.
**What it tests**
• Catching **several correct items** scattered among distractors.
• Hearing **affirmation versus denial**.
**Before the audio**
• Read **all the options** and turn each into a concept to listen for.
• Remember that **most options are decoys**.
• Note **how many answers** are needed.
**During the audio**
• The answers **may not sit next to each other** and rarely come in list order.
• **Keep all options live** until the section ends.
• Tick an option **only when it is clearly affirmed**.
**Traps to watch**
• **Mentioned but denied:** "We thought about a gym, but decided not to."
• **Similar-sounding options** where only one is confirmed.
• **Old versus new:** things that always existed vs things added this year.
• **Free for everyone** vs **included in the ticket**: related, but not the same.
**Beginner vs expert**
• **Beginner:** picks the first two options discussed.
• **Expert:** waits for clear affirmation of each item.
**Worked example**
"Which TWO facilities are new this year?" A) café B) car park C) library D) gym E) garden.
Audio: "We've always had the café and the library. This year we finally added a car park, and the garden is brand new too. A gym was requested but hasn't happened yet."
• Café and library: **old**, not new.
• Gym: **requested, not built**.
• Answers: **B and E**.
**Quick check**
• Have I chosen **exactly the number** asked for?
• Was each choice **affirmed**, not just mentioned?
• Did I hear **a "not" or "hasn't"** attached to any of them?
**Tutor insider tip**
In choose-two questions, listen as hard for "not" and rejection frames as for the items themselves. A denied option is a wrong answer wearing the costume of a right one.

tips.title: Matching
tips.body:
Matching links a list of items, often speakers, to a box of options. Items usually come in order but options jump around, so hold every option's meaning ready and match on who holds the view, not on who spoke last.

**Why it matters:** Matching is common in Part 3, where several voices share opinions. The classic error is attaching the right opinion to the wrong person.
**Recognise it**
• **A list of items** (people, places, stages) matched to **lettered options**.
• Common in **Part 3**, matching speakers to views.
**What it tests**
• **Detailed listening** while tracking several threads at once.
• Knowing **who thinks what**.
**Before the audio**
• Read **the item list and the option box**.
• Check whether **options can be used more than once**.
• Understand **each option's meaning**, since you will hear meaning, not words.
**During the audio**
• Items are usually discussed **in order**; options **jump around**.
• Keep **a finger on the current item**.
• Track **each speaker by name**, noting who agrees and who objects.
**Traps to watch**
• **Options that seem to fit more than one item.**
• **An opinion voiced by one person and agreed by another.**
• **Attaching a view to whoever spoke last.**
• **Abandoned choices:** "I nearly chose X" is not the answer.
**Beginner vs expert**
• **Beginner:** matches the nearest noun to the nearest name.
• **Expert:** matches on **the decision**, tracking the verb of choice.
**Worked example**
Match each student to a topic (climate, migration, housing).
"Aisha: I'm doing housing, though I nearly chose migration. Tom: I've gone for migration. Lena: I was going to do housing too, but Aisha took it, so I'll do climate."
• Aisha: **housing** ("nearly chose" migration is a decoy)
• Tom: **migration**
• Lena: **climate** ("was going to do housing" was abandoned)
**Try one**
Views: i) too expensive ii) well organised iii) too long.
"Ravi: The conference ran smoothly, everything on time. Sara: True, but three full days was more than I needed. Ravi: I didn't mind the length."
• Ravi: **ii**. Sara: **iii**. Nobody mentions cost, so **i is a decoy**.
**Quick check**
• Is each match based on **the final decision**, not the first mention?
• Did I check whether **options can be used more than once**?
• Is there an option that **nobody actually held**?
**Tutor insider tip**
Match on the decision, never on the nearest word. Listen for the verb that shows a final choice: doing, gone for, decided, will.

tips.title: Map Labelling
tips.body:
Map labelling asks you to place locations as a speaker walks you through a map or floor plan. Find the starting point before the audio, then follow the route step by step as the speaker talks.

**Why it matters:** Many candidates freeze on maps because they try to hold the whole plan in their head. The fix is physical: follow the route, one step at a time.
**Recognise it**
• **A map or floor plan** with lettered locations.
• **A list of places** to position on it.
**What it tests**
• Understanding **directions and positions** in real time.
**Before the audio**
• **Orient yourself:** find "you are here" or the entrance.
• Trace **the paths and corridors**.
• Notice **what is already labelled**, since the speaker will use those as landmarks.
**During the audio**
• The speaker takes you **on a route**. Follow it; don't jump ahead.
• **Move your finger or cursor** as they speak.
• Remember that **left and right depend on your direction of travel**.
**Position language to know**
• **opposite, facing, across from**
• **next to, beside, adjacent to**
• **between, in the middle of**
• **at the end of, at the far end**
• **on your left or right, in the corner**
• **just past, beyond, behind, in front of**
• **turn left or right, go straight on**
**Traps to watch**
• **A corrected direction:** "go left, sorry, right".
• **A route described out of order.**
• **Left/right confusion** after a turn.
**Beginner vs expert**
• **Beginner:** stops tracking the route and guesses from the map.
• **Expert:** physically follows the described route.
**Worked example**
Find the gift shop. "Come in through the main entrance. The café is immediately on your right. Walk straight past it, and the gift shop is the second door on your left, just before the exit."
• Start at **the main entrance**.
• Pass **the café on your right**.
• Count doors on the left: the **second one** is the gift shop.
**Try one**
Find the first aid room. "From the reception, head down the main corridor. Pass the toilets on your left, and the first aid room is right at the end, facing you."
• Answer: **at the far end of the main corridor, facing you**, past the toilets on the left.
• "Right at the end, facing you" is **the key position phrase**.
**Tutor insider tip**
Put your finger or cursor on the "you are here" point before the audio starts and move it as the speaker gives directions. Candidates who track the route rarely get lost; candidates who stare at the whole map usually do.

tips.title: Diagram Labelling
tips.body:
Diagram labelling asks you to name the parts of an object, machine or process. Study how the parts connect before the audio, then use position and function clues to place each label, even when the word is new to you.

**Why it matters:** Diagrams bring technical vocabulary that can make candidates freeze. But you rarely need to know the word already: position and function give you the answer.
**Recognise it**
• **A picture** of an object, machine, building or process.
• **Parts to be labelled**, sometimes from a list.
• Common in **Part 4** and **technical Part 2** talks.
**What it tests**
• Matching **spoken descriptions** of position, function and shape to parts of an image.
**Before the audio**
• Study **how the parts relate** to each other.
• Predict **the kind of word** each label needs.
• Guess **the order** the speaker will describe things in.
**During the audio**
• Speakers usually describe **in a logical order**: top to bottom, outside to inside, or order of use.
• Listen for **position language:** at the top, in the centre, at the base.
• Listen for **function language:** this is where water enters, this part holds.
**Useful function phrases**
• **enters through, flows into:** an inlet or entry point
• **is stored in, collects in:** a chamber or tank
• **leaves through, is released from:** an outlet or exit
• **is controlled by, is held by:** a valve, handle or support
**Traps to watch**
• **Unfamiliar technical words.**
• **Parts described by function** rather than named directly.
• **Losing orientation** on the diagram.
**Beginner vs expert**
• **Beginner:** freezes on an unfamiliar word and misses the next two labels.
• **Expert:** uses position and function clues to place a part even when the word is new.
**Worked example**
Label the "outlet" on a water filter (inlet at the top, chamber in the middle, tap at the bottom).
Audio: "Water enters through the inlet at the top, passes down through the filtering chamber in the centre, and finally leaves through the outlet at the very bottom."
• Position: **"at the very bottom"**
• Function: **"water leaves through"**
• Both point to the same part, even if "outlet" is a new word.
**Quick check**
• Does each label sit where **the position words** placed it?
• Does it match **what that part does**?
• Did I keep up with **the speaker's order** of description?
**Tutor insider tip**
An unknown word is not a lost mark. Note where the part sits and what it does, place it, and move on before the next label arrives.

tips.title: Short-Answer Questions
tips.body:
Short-answer questions ask a direct question to be answered in a few words. Predict the answer's shape from the question word, answer exactly what is asked, and trim to the word limit.

**Why it matters:** Short answers look simple, but they carry the same distractors as completion tasks, plus the temptation to write too much.
**Recognise it**
• **A direct question:** "What time does the museum close?"
• A **stated word limit**, often two or three words.
**What it tests**
• Catching **a specific fact**.
• Reporting it **concisely**.
**Before the audio**
• Predict the shape from the **question word**:
• **What:** a thing or an action
• **Where:** a place
• **When:** a time or a date
• **How much / how many:** a number
• **Who:** a person or a role
• Check whether it asks for **one thing or two** ("Name TWO items").
**During the audio**
• Listen for **the specific fact** and let surrounding detail slide past.
• **Respect the word limit strictly.**
**Traps to watch**
• **Corrections and two-option choices**, just as in completion.
• **Related detail** that answers a nearby question, not this one.
• **Standard vs optional:** "a one-year guarantee, extendable to three years for a fee".
**Beginner vs expert**
• **Beginner:** writes a full phrase, or answers a related detail.
• **Expert:** answers the precise question word and trims to the limit.
**Worked example**
"What must visitors leave at reception?" (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS)
Audio: "Before the tour, everyone needs to hand in any large bags at reception, though small handbags are fine to keep."
• "Hand in" = **leave**.
• Answer: **large bags**.
• "Small handbags are fine" is a **related-information decoy**.
**Try one**
"How long is the guarantee?" (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER)
Audio: "It comes with a one-year guarantee as standard, and you can extend it to three years for a small fee."
• Answer: **one year**. Three years is the paid extension, not the standard.
**Tutor insider tip**
Answer the question word, nothing more. If the question asks "where", your answer must be a place, and three words under a two-word limit is wrong.

tips.title: Signposting
tips.body:
Signposts are the small words that tell you what the speaker is about to do. Words like but, actually and sorry warn you that what you just heard is being replaced, so the real answer comes next.

**Why it matters:** You cannot see structure in audio. Signposts are your only map, telling you where the answer is and keeping you oriented through long talks.
**Two jobs signposts do**
• **They locate the answer.** "The main thing to remember is" means the answer is in the next breath.
• **They keep you oriented.** In a Part 4 lecture that runs for minutes, they tell you where you are.
**The signal map**
• **first, then, next, after that:** ordering points. Expect a new answer in sequence.
• **also, in addition, as well as:** adding a point. Often a second item in a list.
• **but, however, although:** contrasting. The real point is usually the second half.
• **actually, in fact, to be honest:** correcting an assumption. The true information follows.
• **sorry, no, I mean, or rather:** self-correction. The answer is what comes after.
• **instead, rather than:** replacing an option. The chosen option follows.
• **the main reason, the key point:** flagging importance. The answer is right here.
• **because, so, as a result:** cause or result. Expect a reason or a consequence.
• **finally, to sum up, overall:** concluding. A final or summary point.
• **moving on, turning to, as for:** changing topic. You are on the next question.
**The shape that hides most answers**
**[wrong or old information] + [signal] + [right or new information]**
• "We usually meet in the library, **but** this week it's in Room 12."
• Decoy: library. Signal: but. **Answer: Room 12.**
**Signposts in Part 3**
• With several speakers, they mark **who agrees, who disagrees and who changes their mind**.
• Listen for: "I'm not so sure", "that's a fair point, but", "I used to think so, though now".
• Part 3 questions often ask what one person thinks, so **these shifts are the whole game**.
**Worked example**
Question: the café's closing time. Audio: "It's open all day, closing at five, **though on Fridays** it stays open until eight."
• "Though on Fridays" marks eight as **a special case**.
• Unless the question says Friday, **the answer is five**.
• The decoy was the later, more memorable number.
**How to use them**
• **Hear the signal, then hold your pen** until the clause after it lands.
• In long talks, use topic-change signals to **move your eyes to the next question**.
• Treat importance signals as **"write now"**.
**Tutor insider tip**
Train yourself to react to but, actually, however, sorry and instead. The moment one lands, assume the answer you were about to write is now the decoy, and wait for the correction.

tips.title: The Distractor Masterclass
tips.body:
Hearing a word is not the same as that word being the answer. The exam says the wrong option out loud on purpose, usually first. Slow your trigger by one clause and most traps disappear.

**Why it matters:** Distractors are how the exam separates Band 6 from Band 8. Both candidates hear the same words; only one knows which are bait.
**The one move behind every trap**
• The exam **deliberately says the wrong option out loud** so a passive listener grabs it.
• The first plausible thing you hear is, more often than not, **the decoy**.
**The 14 distractor types**
• **Correction:** "Room 214, sorry, 240." Treat sorry or actually as overwrite.
• **Two numbers:** "Fifty last year, but sixty now." Find the condition that selects one.
• **Two dates:** opened vs extended. Match the date to the exact thing asked.
• **Two times:** start vs arrival vs closing. Tie each time to its action.
• **Two locations:** old vs new place. "Now" or "instead" marks the current one.
• **Two names:** main contact vs a backup "if he's away". Check the condition.
• **Similar options:** A and B both discussed. **Mention is not endorsement.**
• **Related information:** true detail that doesn't fit the gap. Relevant is not the answer.
• **The example trap:** "warm clothing: hat, gloves, scarf". Category or item? Check the limit.
• **Opinion vs fact:** decide which one the question wants before the audio.
• **Speaker disagreement:** the right opinion attached to the wrong person. Track voices.
• **Changed decision:** the group agrees, then reverses. **The last agreed version wins.**
• **Rejected option:** "We considered a boat trip, but ruled it out."
• **Negation:** "The morning session **isn't** the busy one." One "not" flips the meaning.
**Three heads, one moment**
When does the speaker recommend visiting the castle? A) summer B) spring C) winter.
The speaker criticises summer, then spring, then says "if you ask me... winter".
• **Beginner:** picks summer the moment it is heard.
• **Experienced:** reaches winter, but tempted along the way.
• **Expert:** knew all three would be named, so listened **only for verdict words**.
**The defusing checklist**
Run this silently on any answer you are unsure of:
• Did the speaker **finish the thought**, or could a correction still come?
• Was there **a signal word** that cancels what I heard?
• Does this answer **the exact question**, or just something related?
• Did the speaker **endorse** this option, or merely mention it?
• Was there **a "not" or a rejection** I missed?
• In Part 3, am I sure **which speaker** said it?
If any answer is uncertain, **wait one more clause** before committing.
**Tutor insider tip**
The exam almost always says the wrong answer out loud before it says the right one. Slow your trigger finger by one clause and most distractors disappear.

tips.title: Special Listening Problems
tips.body:
Spelling, numbers, dates, accents and fast speech cost good candidates marks in every test. Know the alphabet and numbers by sound, write digits as you hear them, and when you lose your place, rejoin at the next landmark.

**Why it matters:** A misspelled answer is a wrong answer. These small technical problems quietly cost good candidates a whole band, and every one has a concrete fix.
**Spelling**
• Names and unusual words are often **spelled letter by letter**. Write them **in rough capitals** as they come.
• Watch the pairs that sound alike: **B/P, D/T, G/J, V/B, M/N**, and the vowels **E/I/A**.
• "**Double**" means two of that letter. Listen for **a confirming second pass**.
**Numbers**
• **-teen vs -ty:** thir**TEEN** stresses the end; **THIR**ty stresses the front.
• **Digit strings:** write each digit as you hear it. Never hold a long number in your head.
• "**Double**" means two of the next digit; "**triple**" means three.
• "**Nought point five**" or "zero point five" is 0.5.
**Dates and years**
• The order varies: "the third of March" = "March the third".
• 1985 is "nineteen eighty-five"; 2005 is "two thousand and five" or "twenty oh five".
• Write years as **four digits** unless told otherwise.
**Addresses and phone numbers**
• Expect **number, then street, then postcode**. House numbers are a favourite spot for **corrections**.
• In British English, 0 is usually "**oh**". Write phone numbers as **one continuous string**.
**Accents and fast speech**
• IELTS uses **British, North American, Australian, New Zealand** and other accents. The content words still carry the meaning.
• In fast speech, **stop trying to catch every word**. Listen for **stressed content words**, which stay clear.
**Unfamiliar words**
• **Do not freeze.** Context and the gap's predicted shape usually let you catch the answer anyway.
**Losing concentration or your place**
• Use **question numbers as anchors** to pull your focus back.
• Listen for **the next name, number or signpost** and match it to a question. The audio order does the rest.
• **Never reconstruct** what you missed. Rejoin at the next landmark.
**Part 3 speakers and long options**
• **Fix each speaker by name and voice** at the start.
• With long multiple-choice options, **read all the stems first**, then read the options as the audio approaches each one.
**Tutor insider tip**
Learn the English alphabet by sound until it is automatic, especially the confusable pairs. In the exam you will not have time to think "was that a G or a J?"

tips.title: The Recovery System
tips.body:
The cost of a missed answer is not the answer: it is the answers you miss while chasing it. Recognise, leave, reset, follow, then recover with a guess at the end. One miss should stay one miss.

**Why it matters:** Missing question 5 costs one mark. Chasing it while the audio delivers 6 and 7 costs three. This cascade, not the original miss, separates a 6 from an 8.
**The principle**
• **Protect the future by abandoning the past instantly.**
• High scorers still miss answers. Their misses **stay contained to a single mark**.
**How the cascade happens**
• You miss question 5.
• Your mind stays on it, replaying what you heard.
• The audio delivers **6 and 7** while you are looking backwards.
• One miss has become **three**.
**The five-step Recovery System**
• **RECOGNISE.** Notice, calmly, that the answer has gone. No emotion, just a fact.
• **LEAVE.** Let it go completely. Put a small mark by the question number.
• **RESET.** Bring your attention fully to the present. That question is closed.
• **FOLLOW.** Move your eyes to the next question and rejoin the audio at that landmark.
• **RECOVER.** In the final review, return to marked questions and make your best guess.
**The hard step**
• **LEAVE** is the hardest, because the instinct is to chase.
• Learn to **feel the chase starting** and drop it on purpose.
**Why you always guess**
• There is **no penalty** for wrong answers.
• **A guess can score. A blank cannot.**
• Use the predicted shape and the answers around it to make the guess **sensible**.
**In action**
You are on question 12 and realise you missed 11 while writing 10.
• **Recognise** that 11 is lost.
• **Leave** it with a light mark.
• **Reset** and **follow** the audio into 12.
• **Recover** 11 with a guess in the final review.
Sacrificing 11 to save 12 is **the correct trade**. Trying to save 11 loses both.
**Panic, and the cure**
• Panic is **attention pointed at fear** instead of at the next answer.
• "Calm down" does not work under pressure. **An immediate task does:** eyes to the next question, ear hunting the next target.
**Tutor insider tip**
Practise missing on purpose. In a practice test, when you miss an answer, watch whether your mind chases it, and force the reset.

tips.title: Listening Time Strategy
tips.body:
You cannot control the pace of the audio, only how you use the pauses. Read ahead in every pause, never fall behind, and use the final two minutes to fill blanks and check word limits, in that order.

**Why it matters:** Listening has a fixed rhythm you do not control. Your strategy is entirely about using the time you are given, especially the pauses, with maximum efficiency.
**The shape of every part**
• A voice tells you **which questions to look at**.
• **A short pause** to read them.
• **The audio plays** and you answer.
• You **move on to the next set**.
**Using the pauses**
• Use every pause to **read ahead**: predict shapes, mark keywords, understand options.
• **Never admire answers you already have.** That time belongs to the next set.
• If you finish early, **read into the following set** and bank the time.
**The computer-delivered test**
• **No ten-minute transfer.** You type answers directly.
• About **two minutes** to review at the end.
• **Capture every answer cleanly the first time.** The review is a check, not a rescue.
**The final two minutes, in priority order**
• **Blanks:** fill every one with a best guess.
• **Word limits:** trim any answer that runs over.
• **Spelling** of names and places.
• **Singular or plural**, where the grammar decides it.
**Manage the difficulty curve**
• **Part 1** is the easiest. Bank those marks with full care: they count as much as Part 4.
• Keep your concentration **highest going into Part 4**, the densest section.
**Common time traps**
• **Reviewing old answers** during a pause meant for reading ahead.
• **Rebuilding a lost answer** from memory while the audio moves on.
• **Treating Part 1 as a warm-up** and dropping easy marks.
**The perfect Listening routine**
• **Before the test:** know the format, the alphabet and numbers by sound; practise on screen with varied accents.
• **At the start of each part:** read, predict every gap, mark one keyword per question, pre-load paraphrases.
• **During the audio:** listen for meaning and anchors, write answers at once, wait through distractors.
• **When you miss one:** recognise, leave, reset, follow.
• **Between parts:** read into the next set.
• **At the end:** fill blanks, trim to limits, fix spellings, check plurals.
**Tutor insider tip**
The pauses are your only preparation time. A candidate who spends them re-checking old answers walks into every part cold.

tips.title: The Practice Ladder and Error Log
tips.body:
Strategy that is only read is forgotten; strategy that is practised becomes instinct. Climb seven levels from understanding to full timed tests, and give every mistake a reason so you know exactly what to fix.

**Why it matters:** Reading about strategy feels productive but changes little. Practice turns decisions into reflexes, and the Error Log tells you which reflex needs work.
**The seven-level ladder**
• **Understand:** a quick self-check on the core ideas.
• **Guided practice:** prediction, keyword and paraphrase drills.
• **Independent practice:** single question types, on your own.
• **Trap practice:** every item hides a distractor.
• **Mixed practice:** a Part 1 style mini-test.
• **Mixed question types:** a Part 3 style mini-test.
• **Full test:** real audio, real speed, played once.
**Self-check: can you answer these?**
• What do you ask of **every gap**? What kind of answer am I about to hear?
• Which words are **almost never paraphrased**? Names, numbers, dates.
• In **[decoy] + [signal] + [answer]**, where is the answer? After the signal.
• What does hearing an option's words tell you? Almost nothing, until it is endorsed.
• What must you never do after a miss? Chase it.
**Rules for full tests**
• **Predict and set anchors** in every pause.
• **Play the audio once.** Never pause or replay in a timed run.
• **Capture answers immediately** and obey word limits.
• Treat **but, actually, sorry, instead** as alarms.
• **Reset cleanly** after a miss.
• Sit full tests **at the same time of day** as your real exam, in one sitting.
**Practising without audio**
• Read short transcripts **once, at speaking pace**, then answer.
• **No rereading**, just as in the real test.
• Move to **real audio** for timed and full tests.
**The Error Log**
• After every practice, give **each wrong answer a reason**, not just a cross.
• Typical reasons: **spelling, missed correction, word limit, distractor, lost place, wrong speaker**.
• Count them every week. **Drill the reason that dominates.**
**The mindset in one breath**
• **Before:** predict every gap and set your anchors.
• **During:** listen for meaning, ride the signposts, wait for the verdict.
• **After a miss:** reset and move on without looking back.
• **Afterwards:** log every mistake by reason.
**Tutor insider tip**
Do your full tests in one sitting, with no pausing, at the same time of day as your real exam. Your brain needs to rehearse the stamina, not just the questions.
