articles.title: True, False or Not Given: 4 rules that stop guessing
articles.meta: Reading Tips · 5 min read · updated Sep 2026

tips.title: Treat each statement as a claim
tips.body: Read the statement and ask one question: does the passage agree, disagree or say nothing? Underline the key idea — a number, a comparison, a cause — because that is what you are checking.

tips.title: Find the matching sentence
tips.body: The statements follow the order of the passage. Scan for names, dates or unusual words, then read the sentence around them slowly. The answer is almost never spread across several paragraphs.

tips.title: False means the opposite
tips.body: Choose False only when the passage clearly contradicts the statement: “rose” versus “fell”, “all” versus “some”, “before” versus “after”. A missing detail is not a contradiction.

tips.title: Not Given means silent
tips.body: If the passage mentions the topic but not the specific claim, the answer is Not Given. Never fill the gap with general knowledge, however obvious the fact seems.

tips.body: Skim the list of headings before the passage and note how they differ. Two headings often share a word, so decide what makes each one unique.

tips.title: Ignore matching single words

tips.title: Check the word limit
tips.body: “NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS” means one or two words only. Numbers written as figures count as one word. Going over the limit scores zero, even if the idea is right.

tips.title: Locate the section
tips.body: Summaries usually cover one part of the passage. Find where the first gap’s idea appears and stay in that section — the answers follow the text in order.

tips.body: The question stem tells you exactly what to find — a reason, a purpose, an opinion. Underline it before you look at the options.

articles.title: Five pillars: accuracy, vocabulary and sentences
articles.meta: Writing Tips · 2 min read · from the nextED Writing guide

tips.title: Hunt your own spelling mistakes
tips.body: Make a list of the 10 words you yourself misspell again and again, and in the last 2–3 minutes of the exam look for just those. Small slips (teh / recieve) do little harm, but a spelling mistake that changes the meaning (advice / advise, then / than, lose / loose) is treated as using the wrong word — far more serious.

tips.title: Fix the five basic grammar errors first
tips.body: Tense, subject–verb agreement, singular/plural, adjective/adverb and unclear pronouns tell the examiner your foundation is weak (The number of cars has increased; Sales rose significantly). Fix these five before thinking about "advanced" grammar: 15 simple but correct sentences get a higher band than 10 complex sentences with 6 mistakes.

tips.title: Upgrade words only when you are sure
tips.body: Replace a common word with a more precise one only if you are sure it is correct (a big problem → a serious / significant problem), because an uncommon word used wrongly loses more marks than a common word used correctly. To avoid repeating words, write two synonyms for each key noun of the question on the question paper before you start (children → young people, minors).

tips.title: A correct simple sentence always wins
tips.body: Mix simple, compound and complex sentences — roughly one complex sentence after every two simple/compound ones. Golden rule: if you are not sure, break the long sentence into two short ones and join them with a linking word. Never use a double connector: not "Although it was raining, but we went out".

tips.title: Write active; use passive only when needed
tips.body: The passive does not make writing "academic" — the active voice is direct, clear and strong (My friends have supported the decision). Use the passive only when the doer is unimportant, unknown or deliberately hidden, for a polite suggestion, or to describe a process, as in a Task 1 flow chart (The beans are roasted, then ground).

articles.title: Coherence and linking words: make your writing flow
articles.meta: Writing Tips · 2 min read · from the nextED Writing guide

tips.title: One paragraph, one topic sentence
tips.body: Start every paragraph with a specific topic sentence ("People move to cities for three main reasons.", not the vague "Many people move to cities.") and make every other sentence support it. To check, cover everything except the topic sentence and ask of each sentence: "Does this support the topic sentence?" If not, cut it or move it — drifting away from the topic is a very costly mistake.

tips.title: Keep paragraphs a readable size
tips.body: Long paragraphs tire the reader: 80–150 words (roughly 5–8 lines) is ideal, and beyond 200 words the reader loses the thread. A one-sentence emphatic paragraph can be used very rarely — never in Task 1.

tips.title: One connective every two or three sentences
tips.body: Connectives such as First, However, As a result and For example tell the reader what kind of sentence comes next, and IELTS gives marks for this directly. But if every sentence starts with one, the writing sounds mechanical and gets stuck at band 6. Pick 2–3 words from each function and use them until they feel natural.

tips.title: Match the connective to the logic
tips.body: Moreover before an opposing point, or As a result before something that is not a result, shows the examiner you do not understand the word. A connective at the start of a sentence takes a comma (However, …), while whereas / while / although join two clauses inside one sentence.

tips.title: Phrases to drop for good
tips.body: Never write "According to me" — write In my view / In my opinion / I believe. Do not use "At last" (it means after a long wait), and do not start a conclusion with "Last but not least". On the contrary does not mean on the other hand; use it only to reject a mistaken idea: He is not lazy; on the contrary, he works twelve hours a day.

articles.title: Task 1: 5 red lines that cost bands
articles.meta: Writing Tips · 2 min read · from the nextED Writing guide

tips.title: 150 is the floor, about 180 the target
tips.body: Never write fewer than 150 words — even 148 loses marks — and don't go above 200, or not more than 20 minutes: more words mean more mistakes and less time for Task 2, which carries double the weight. Don't count in the exam hall; find out beforehand how many lines 170 words take in your handwriting (usually 12–14).

tips.title: Overview goes second, with no numbers
tips.body: Write four paragraphs: introduction, overview, and two body paragraphs with numbers. Put the overview (the 2–3 biggest features, without numbers) right after the introduction — if it is left for the end and you run out of time, a whole band is lost in Task Achievement. A conclusion is optional, and if you write one it is a summary, never an opinion.

tips.title: No opinion, no I, we, you
tips.body: Task 1 only tests whether you can describe the given data, so any opinion, advice or explanation of why something happened ("probably because of the pandemic") lowers Task Achievement. The report is impersonal: write The chart shows…, never We can see… or You can notice….

tips.title: Understand the graph before you write
tips.body: Read the title, both axis labels, the unit and the legend, and ask: what is measured, in which unit, over what period, how many categories? Start writing only when you can explain it to yourself in one sentence — otherwise you end up describing the wrong thing. Spend about the first 3 minutes on this.

tips.title: Match the tense to the time
tips.body: The first sentence (The graph shows…) is always present. Past years → past tense (Sales rose in 2010); no year → present; future years → not will but is expected / projected / forecast to + verb (Solar output is expected to triple by 2030). Process and diagram → present simple, usually passive.

articles.title: Task 1: overview, trends and comparisons
articles.meta: Writing Tips · 2 min read · from the nextED Writing guide

tips.title: Build the overview from the big picture
tips.body: The overview gives the 2–3 biggest points without numbers: the overall direction (increased / decreased / fluctuated), the highest and lowest, the position at the end compared with the start, any major exception (a big slump, a crossover), and with several lines who is at the top and bottom at the end. For a map, it is the overall character of the change — including what stayed the same.

tips.title: Select and group — no data dump
tips.body: Pick 4–6 key points (start, end, peak, trough, crossover, biggest change), not every number. Arrange the data by behaviour — the big ones, the small ones, the ones that changed, and the exception — not left to right or row by row. Express numbers as relationships where possible: nearly doubled, a third, almost level with.

tips.title: One trend sentence, one clear formula
tips.body: Use Subject + verb + adverb + time + amount: Visitor numbers + rose + sharply + between 1995 and 2005 + to 480,000. Every trend sentence needs direction, degree, number and time, and no verb, adverb or connective should appear three times. Check your prepositions: by / to / at / from…to.

tips.title: No rise or fall without time
tips.body: Bars of categories and a single pie do not "rise" or "fall" — write X is higher than Y, X has the largest share, accounts for. A pie does not grow; the share of a segment does. From 25% to 40% is a rise of 15 percentage points, not 15 percent, and several pies are compared segment by segment.

tips.title: Processes and maps: follow the arrows
tips.body: In a process, describe by following the arrows in the present simple (man-made → passive), vary the sequencers instead of "Then… Then…", and add nothing that is not in the diagram. In a map, compare the changes rather than writing two inventories, give compass directions, and use past for a past map and will be built for a plan.

articles.title: Task 2: ground rules and planning
articles.meta: Writing Tips · 2 min read · from the nextED Writing guide

tips.title: 260–290 words in 40 minutes
tips.body: Never go below 250 words (even 248 is a penalty), and above 320 there is no gain — mistakes simply increase. Spend 0–5 minutes reading, deciding the type, brainstorming and planning, 5–35 writing and 35–40 revising: skipping the plan makes a paragraph lose direction, skipping revision leaves easy mistakes behind, and each costs half a band.

tips.title: Identify the question type first
tips.body: Read the question twice and underline the topic words and the instruction words separately — the type decides what goes in the conclusion. Argumentative: write the arguments of both sides and give an opinion in the conclusion. Narrative: write only what is asked; only a suggestion at the end. Combination: answer both questions, in separate paragraphs.

tips.title: Brainstorm before you pick a side
tips.body: Brainstorm on the question paper in two columns and do not stop until you have at least 3 points on one side; write weak ideas too, since selection comes later. Choose your side only after brainstorming: the side with the stronger arguments becomes yours, so the essay is automatically strong. In fact, the essay has already been made in the brainstorm.

tips.title: Introduction: general statement + thesis
tips.body: Write 2–3 sentences (40–55 words) with no argument yet: a general statement about the subject, then a thesis with your position, a hint of the main reason and, optionally, the other side with a softener. "This essay will discuss…" without your view is not a thesis, and do not start with a question.

tips.title: What never belongs in Task 2
tips.body: No memorised essays (the examiner recognises them at a glance), no contractions, slang or "etc.", and no headings, bullets or numbering — full sentences, full paragraphs. Don't use grammar or words you are not sure of: if not confident, write simple sentences and join them with linking words. One irrelevant sentence is forgiven, one irrelevant paragraph is not.

articles.title: Task 2: body paragraphs, conclusion and essay types
articles.meta: Writing Tips · 2 min read · from the nextED Writing guide

tips.title: Topic sentence, explanation, example
tips.body: Every body paragraph has one idea: a topic sentence that states its main claim, 1–2 sentences of explanation if needed, and one concrete example (a country, an event, a common situation). Aim for 70–100 words per paragraph. A template is only a skeleton — fill it with content from your own topic.

tips.title: Emphasise your side, soften theirs
tips.body: In an argumentative essay use emphasisers (undoubtedly, clearly, the main, crucial) in your own points and softeners (may, some, arguably, it is sometimes claimed that) in the opposing points — every time. Present the other side and answer it: Although some shop owners may lose a little trade at first, a car-free centre undoubtedly attracts far more visitors in the long run.

tips.title: A short conclusion with your opinion
tips.body: In 1–2 sentences (30–45 words): a concluding connective plus your opinion in new words, and a suggestion if you like. Do not bring in a new argument, copy the thesis word for word, suddenly turn "balanced", end with a question, write "Thank you" or start with "Last but not least".

tips.title: Narrative: only what has been asked
tips.body: If the question is "What are the problems of tourism?", a paragraph on benefits is off-topic and costs a band. Use neutral language and give no opinion unless asked; a suggestion at the end is fine. In a problem–solution essay every solution must fix a problem you stated (cheap fast food → a tax or labelling, not "build more gyms").

tips.title: Combination: answer both questions
tips.body: Give each question its own body paragraph and roughly equal weight — not the first in detail and the second in one sentence. Mention both parts in the introduction and close both in the conclusion, restating your opinion for the argumentative part. It is one essay, with one introduction and one conclusion.

articles.title: 10 Speaking Tips (Part 1 of 2)
articles.meta: Speaking Tips · 2 min read · from the nextED Speaking guide

tips.title: Practise pronunciation daily
tips.body: Pronunciation is one of the four criteria, so it is 25% of your score. It won't change in a week, but 10 minutes a day for four weeks makes a clear difference. Each day, say one hard sound pair (like vest–west) 20 times and one sentence with correct stress 5 times, out loud.

tips.title: Extend your answers
tips.body: "Yes." "No." "Sometimes." — one-word answers give the examiner nothing to mark. Give at least one reason and one detail in every answer. Practise any Part 1 question in no fewer than 2 and no more than 4 sentences, and record yourself.

tips.title: Master the Part 2 structure
tips.body: Without a structure you run out of things to say in 40 seconds. Follow the card's points in a fixed order — what, when/where, why, feelings — and any topic fills 2 minutes. Practise a cue card with a timer; if you stop before 1:30, do it again.

tips.title: Use advanced vocabulary naturally
tips.body: "Advanced" doesn't mean difficult, it means precise — not "good" but "rewarding", not "very tired" but "exhausted". The word must sound like your own; a big word in the wrong place lowers your Lexical Resource. Listen to a recorded answer, mark every very/good/bad/thing, replace them and say it again.

tips.title: Handle Part 3 abstract questions
tips.body: Part 3 asks about society, the future, causes and effects — not about you. There is no "right" answer; there is opinion + reason + example + the other side. Practise by speaking for 30 seconds from each side on one social topic a day (traffic, online learning, tourism).

articles.title: 10 Speaking Tips (Part 2 of 2)
articles.meta: Speaking Tips · 2 min read · from the nextED Speaking guide

tips.title: Fix common grammar mistakes
tips.body: Our mistakes aren't random — the same ten or twelve errors from Bangla grammar keep coming back (I am agree, cousin brother, he/she, since + present). Catch these and your accuracy jumps at once. Read the ten correct sentences aloud once a day until the mistake starts to sound wrong to you.

tips.title: Manage your nervousness
tips.body: Nervousness doesn't take away your English — it takes away your access to it. The cure is preparation and familiarity: know the format, know your first minute, and know what to say when you pause. Do a full 12-minute mock test with a friend as the examiner at least three times; by the third, the fear is halved.

tips.title: Use idiomatic expressions carefully
tips.body: Band 7 asks for "some idiomatic vocabulary" — everyday phrases (be into, get by, once in a blue moon), not proverbs. Use at most one per answer, and only ones you have used many times. Take 3 phrases a week and use each in 3 sentences about your own life.

tips.title: Build fluency through shadowing
tips.body: Shadowing means speaking along with native audio at the same speed, stress and tone. It builds fluency, pronunciation and natural phrasing together — the practice with the biggest return. Take 30 seconds of a podcast or interview: listen once, shadow it 3 times, 10 minutes a day.

tips.title: Prepare topic-specific vocabulary
tips.body: There are hundreds of Speaking topics but only 20–25 categories (work, education, environment, technology, health...). With 10–15 of your own words and collocations ready for each category, words come even for unfamiliar questions. Copy 5 words or phrases from each topic's model answer into your notebook and use them in your own sentences.

articles.title: Fluency & Pronunciation: Flow and Clarity
articles.meta: Speaking Tips · 2 min read · from the nextED Speaking guide

tips.title: Fluency is flow, not speed
tips.body: Being fluent doesn't mean speaking fast — rushing blurs your pronunciation and breaks your grammar. A good speaker talks at a natural pace, without stopping or stumbling. Fluency breaks on three things: hesitation, repetition and self-correction.

tips.title: Pause with English phrases, not "umm"
tips.body: Pausing isn't forbidden; native speakers pause too. Silence or "umm/aaa" hurts fluency, but a phrase like "Well,", "Let me think for a second." or "...what's the word..." sounds natural and gives you time to think. Use them like an umbrella — only when needed, about once every 3–4 answers, and vary them.

tips.title: Correct only mistakes that change meaning
tips.body: If a mistake changes your meaning, fix it briefly: "...sorry, I mean I didn't like it." If it's a small grammar slip (article, -s, tense), don't go back — the examiner would hear the mistake plus a hesitation. Keep going.

tips.title: Link your ideas, but don't overuse linkers
tips.body: Linking words turn a list into an argument. In Speaking, conversational forms (I'd say, the thing is, having said that, at the end of the day) sound more natural than Writing forms like Moreover or Furthermore. Use a linker only when you really need to show how two ideas connect; starting every sentence with one is a Band 6 sign.

tips.title: Clarity matters, not accent
tips.body: IELTS doesn't want a British, American or Australian accent — pronunciation measures how easily the listener understands you. Even Band 8 allows a first-language accent if it doesn't block understanding. Work on hard sounds (vest–west, sip–ship), word stress (de-VEL-op, ho-TEL), sentence stress and intonation.

articles.title: Part 1: Length, Strategies and Rules
articles.meta: Speaking Tips · 2 min read · from the nextED Speaking guide

tips.title: Don't take Part 1 lightly
tips.body: The examiner forms a first impression in the first two minutes, and it's hard to change later. Getting stuck on "What do you do in your free time?" suggests weak basic fluency. A good Part 1 also relaxes you for Part 2.

tips.title: Answer in 2 to 4 sentences
tips.body: One word or one sentence gives the examiner no chance to hear your English. Talking for a minute gets you stopped. Answer + reason + one detail is the right size: "Yes, pretty much every day, actually. I take the bus to work since it's by far the cheapest option."

tips.title: Pick one of three strategies
tips.body: No reason asked (what/where/how long) → Direct Answer + Extension. A like, opinion or hidden "why" → A.R.E (Answer – Reason – Example). Habits or free time → L.D.F (Likes – Frequency – Reason). When in doubt, use A.R.E — it works everywhere.

tips.title: Answer first, and don't echo the question
tips.body: Your first word should be Yes/No/Sort of/It depends — no introduction. Don't just repeat the question's words: "Yes, I'm quite into it, actually" beats "Yes, I like cooking." Never stop at Yes/No; add because, since or the thing is.

tips.title: Add a concrete detail and vary your words
tips.body: "I like music — mostly old Bangla band songs from the nineties" gives the examiner far more language than "I like music". Replace 'very' with quite, pretty, fairly, absolutely or not particularly, and keep present-tense -s correct (she works, it takes). Give the answer that has more to say — truth isn't checked.

articles.title: Part 2: Notes, Structure and Filling 2 Minutes
articles.meta: Speaking Tips · 2 min read · from the nextED Speaking guide

tips.title: Write 4 + 1 keywords, not sentences
tips.body: In one minute you can write two sentences at most, and then you'd read them out — reading, not speaking. Writing nothing is also a mistake; nervous, you'll forget the third point. Write one keyword per card line plus one extra sensory detail — five words in capitals, top to bottom.

tips.title: Split your one minute
tips.body: 0–10 seconds: read the whole card and choose one thing, person or event — the first that comes to mind with the most to say. 10–40: write the 4 keywords. 40–50: add the + detail. 50–60: say your first sentence in your head.

tips.title: Follow the five-step talk
tips.body: Opening (~10s): "The skill I've chosen is...". Bullets 1 & 2 (~35s): background in the past tense. Bullet 3 (~35s): how it happened — the story. Explain (~30s): feelings and why it matters, back in the present. Closing (~10s): "So, all in all...".

tips.title: Use lenses to fill 2 minutes
tips.body: If you think you have nothing to say, look through six lenses: time, senses, people, contrast, a moment and meaning. Senses and contrast are your own additions — they turn Band 6 into Band 7. If you run dry, check your note for an unused keyword, switch lens ("Thinking about it now, ..."), or close neatly after 1:20.

tips.title: Avoid the common Part 2 mistakes
tips.body: Don't answer each bullet in one sentence — treat each as 2–4 sentences. Stay personal and specific, not general; memorise the structure, not the content. Keep past stories in past tense, look at the examiner 80% of the time, and give the "explain" line its full 30 seconds.

articles.title: Part 3: A.R.E + Balance and Hedging
articles.meta: Speaking Tips · 2 min read · from the nextED Speaking guide

tips.title: Use A.R.E + Balance
tips.body: Answer with a clear opinion, give a Reason, add an Example, then Balance with the other side: "Having said that..." / "Of course, it depends...". The Balance step shows you can see more than one side and use complex grammar — this is a Band 7 Part 3 answer.

tips.title: Give longer answers than Part 1
tips.body: There is no right answer and no answer key; the opinion you can explain best is the right one. Part 3 answers are 4–6 sentences, 30–45 seconds. Don't stop after two sentences — the examiner will stop you if needed.

tips.title: Hedge your opinions
tips.body: "Governments must ban cars" sounds immature; "I think governments should probably look at restricting cars in city centres" sounds thoughtful. Say "People tend to be less active than they used to be" rather than "People are lazy now". Band 7+ needs this hedging.

tips.title: When you don't know, keep talking
tips.body: Silence is not an option, but all three routes are: guess with a reason ("I'd imagine... because..."), generalise from what you've seen, or narrow the question ("It probably depends a lot on the country. In mine, ..."). You can't stop at "I don't know", but you can say "I don't know, but..." and continue.

tips.title: Avoid the common Part 3 mistakes
tips.body: Talk about people in general ("most families", "in my country"), keeping your own story for the Example step. Use one filler phrase at most, then answer directly. If the examiner challenges you, hold your view: "That's a fair point, but I'd still say...".

The line graph illustrates the proportion of households which had access to the internet in Canada, Brazil and India from 2000 to 2020.

Overall, internet access rose steadily in all three countries over the period. Canada had the highest figures throughout, while India had the lowest, although it showed the biggest growth at the end.

In 2000, 42% of Canadian homes were connected, which was more than double the figure for Brazil (18%) and much higher than India, where only 9% of households had access. Over the next ten years, Canada increased to 66% and Brazil rose quickly to 47%. India grew more slowly and reached 24% in 2010.

From 2010 to 2020, the growth continued in every country. Canada reached 82% by the end of the period, and Brazil climbed to 72%, so the gap between them became smaller. writing.task2:
Nowadays more and more companies allow their staff to work from home, especially after the pandemic. Some people think this arrangement is good for both workers and employers. I mostly agree with this opinion, although I believe there are some disadvantages that should be considered.

On the one hand, working from home has clear benefits for employees. First of all, they do not need to commute every day, so they save a lot of time and money. For example, in big cities like Dhaka, people can spend two or three hours in traffic, and this time could be used for family or rest. In addition, a flexible schedule helps workers to balance their work and personal life, which can make them more satisfied with their job.

On the other hand, employers can also gain from remote work. Companies can reduce their overheads because they need smaller offices and pay less for electricity and rent. Moreover, they can recruit talented people from any location, not only from the city where the office is. This means the talent pool is much bigger than before.

However, there are some drawbacks. Some employees feel isolated when they work alone for a long time, and junior staff may lose the chance to learn from experienced colleagues. Also, the boundary between work and home can become unclear, so people might work longer hours and suffer from burnout.

In conclusion, I believe working from home benefits both employees and employers in many ways, such as saving time and reducing costs. Nevertheless, a hybrid model, where staff come to the office some days, may be the best solution to avoid isolation.

data.text:
Over the past decade, remote work has moved from a rare perk to a mainstream arrangement for many office staff. In my view, working from home offers very good things to both workers and companies, although it is not without drawbacks.

For employees, the most obvious advantage is the time saved on commuting. In a city such as Dhaka, where a single journey can take more than an hour, people who works from home can spend this time with their kids or get some rest before starting work. This tends to improve concentration during working hours. Also, workers are happier. Also they stay longer in the same company.

In the other hand, employers benefit from lower office costs, which mean they can invest more in staff training. A company that no longer rents a big office in the city centre can save a lot of money every year. Moreover, managers can hire talented staff from other cities, which widens the pool of applicants.

Admittedly, some workers feel lonely at home, and it is really difficult for new staff to learn from their colleagues. For instance, a junior accountant may not know who to ask when a question appears. However, regular video meetings and one office day per week can solve most of these difficulties.

In conclusion, I believe that working from home benefits both employees and employers. If companies organise it carefully, the advantages are much greater than the disadvantages, and both sides will be more productive and more satisfied in the long term.

Traffic congestion is a serious problem in many cities around the world. Some people argue that governments should invest in public transport, while others believe that building more roads is the best solution. This essay will discuss both views before giving my opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of new roads say that wider streets allow cars to move faster. In countries where many people already own a car, more roads can reduce journey times in the short term. In addition, roads are essential for delivery trucks, which carry food and other goods to shops.

On the other hand, I think that spending on buses and trains is a better long-term plan. A single train can carry a lot of passengers, so it takes hundreds of cars off the road. Moreover, public transport produces less pollution per person, which is important for the health of people who live in big cities. Studies also show that new roads often fill up with more cars within a few years, so the problem soon returns.

And public transport helps poorer people who cannot afford a car to reach jobs and schools. This makes society more fair and it's good for the economy.

In conclusion, although building roads can give quick relief, I believe governments should spend more money on public transport because it is cheaper, cleaner and fairer in the long run.

The diagram show how water moves around the Earth in a cycle.

First, the sun heats the water in the oceans and it turns into water vapour. This vapour goes up into the sky. When it is high, the air is cold so the vapour becomes small drops of water and makes clouds.

Next, the clouds move over the land with the wind. When the drops get heavy, they fall down as rain or snow. This is called precipitation. Some of the rain runs over the ground into rivers and lakes, and some goes into the soil and becomes groundwater.

Finally the water in rivers and under the ground goes back to the sea. Then the sun heats it again and the whole process starts again from the beginning.

In conclusion, the water cycle has four main stages which are evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection, and it never stops.

transcript.text: Before you head off to explore, I'd like to give you a quick introduction to the building and tell you what you'll find in each area.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: A lot of visitors assume this building was once a fish market, because the fish quay is just outside the front door.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: In fact, it was built in 1842 as the town's customs house, where merchants paid tax on the goods their ships brought in.

answerTags.after: built in 1842 as the town's customs house

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: It only became a museum in the 1970s, after the shipbuilders' warehouse next door was knocked down.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Now, some news for regular visitors. Entry is still seven pounds for adults, I'm afraid, so it hasn't become free, although under-sixteens still get in without paying.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: What has changed is that since April we've extended our opening hours, so we now close at six rather than five.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: We're also hoping to launch an audio guide app, but that won't be ready until next year.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: So, where to start? Most people go straight into the Harbour Gallery, but I'd suggest you begin with the short film in the Orientation Room.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: It's only twelve minutes long and it gives you a timeline that makes everything else much easier to follow.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: A quick practical point: reception no longer has space to store luggage, so any large bags must go in the lockers on the lower ground floor.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Right, the areas themselves. The Harbour Gallery has our collection of oil paintings of the port.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Some of them are very fragile, so please keep your cameras and phones away in there. Photography isn't allowed in that gallery at all.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Next door is the Shipwreck Room. We used to run free guided talks in there, but these days it's self-guided.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The highlight is the original captain's log from the Mary Ellen, along with letters written by her crew, the real documents, not copies.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Then there's the Lighthouse Tower. You can climb all ninety steps, but it costs an extra two pounds on top of your ticket.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: People expect a spectacular view from the top, but to be honest the windows are rather small.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: On the first floor you'll find the Rope Workshop. At eleven and at two, one of our volunteers shows you how rope was made by hand, so you can watch the whole process live.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: If you have children with you, head for the Children's Deck. They can dress up as sailors, try tying knots and steer a model ship, so it's all hands-on.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: I should mention that the Navigation Room on the same floor is temporarily closed while we repair the roof.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: And finally, the Captain's Café on the top floor. The cakes are excellent, but the real reason to go up is the terrace.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: From there you get the best view of the town and the whole harbour, much better than from the tower.

answerTags.after: the best view of the town

transcript.speaker: Guide

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: If you have any questions, you'll find me or one of the other guides in the entrance hall.

transcript.speaker: Guide

sets.title: Urban heat islands
sets.context: A lecturer explains why cities are warmer than the countryside and what can be done about it.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Good afternoon. Today we're looking at a phenomenon that affects almost every large city on the planet: the urban heat island.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Put simply, an urban heat island is a built-up area that is noticeably warmer than the countryside around it.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The effect was first described in the early nineteenth century by Luke Howard, an amateur scientist who is better known for naming the clouds.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Howard kept careful temperature records in London and compared them with readings taken in nearby villages.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So how big is the difference? You will sometimes read that city centres can be twelve degrees warmer, but that figure comes from a single, very unusual night.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: A more typical maximum is around seven degrees, and in most cities the average difference is much smaller.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Interestingly, the gap is not greatest in the middle of a hot afternoon, as you might expect.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: It is actually at night that the difference is most marked, because the city releases the heat it has stored during the day.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: That brings us to the causes. The first is the materials we build with.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Dark surfaces, and asphalt in particular, absorb a great deal of solar energy and then give it off slowly for hours.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Concrete and brick behave in a similar way, though they are generally a little paler.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The second cause is the lack of vegetation. In the countryside, plants and moist soil cool the air through evaporation.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: In a city, rainwater is quickly carried away by drains, so there is far less moisture available for this natural cooling.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The third cause is waste heat. Vehicles contribute, of course, but a surprisingly large share is released by buildings, through heating systems, lighting and machinery.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: And the shape of the city matters too: tall buildings along narrow streets trap warm air and block the wind.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Why does any of this matter? Hotter cities use more energy for cooling, and air pollution tends to be worse.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: But the most serious concern is health. During heatwaves, the group most at risk is the elderly, particularly those who live alone.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Young children are also vulnerable, but studies consistently show the highest death rates among older people.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So what can planners do? One simple approach is so-called cool roofs.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: These are roofs painted white or covered with light materials so that they reflect sunlight rather than absorbing it.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Another is to increase green space. Many people assume that grass is enough, but in fact it provides relatively little cooling.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The most effective measure is planting trees along streets, because they provide shade as well as releasing moisture.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Finally, cities need better data. Here in our own city, researchers originally planned to use weather balloons.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Instead, they attached two hundred small sensors to lampposts, which now record temperature every ten minutes.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The results have already shown which neighbourhoods need the most urgent attention.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: In next week's session we'll look at some of that data in detail, so please read chapter five before then.

sets.title: Sleep and memory
sets.context: A psychology lecture on how sleep helps the brain store memories.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we're looking at one of the most active areas of research in psychology: the relationship between sleep and memory.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: For a long time, sleep was seen as a period when the brain simply switched off. We now know that's far from the truth.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: One of the earliest studies took place in 1924. Two American researchers asked participants to learn lists of nonsense syllables, and then tested them some hours later.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: They found that people remembered considerably more if they had slept during that period than if they had stayed awake.
keywords: than if they had stayed awake

answerTags.after: than if they had stayed awake

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: At the time, the explanation was simply that sleep protected memories from interference. Today we believe sleep does something much more active.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: To understand this, we need to look at two brain regions. The first is the hippocampus. When we experience something new, the memory is initially held there, in what we might call a temporary buffer.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The hippocampus can't hold much information for long, though. It's a bit like a notepad rather than a filing cabinet.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: During deep, slow-wave sleep, memories are gradually transferred from the hippocampus to the cortex, where they can be stored for the long term.
keywords: from the hippocampus to the cortex

answerTags.after: from the hippocampus to the cortex

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Some of the clearest evidence for this comes from animal studies. Researchers recorded the activity of individual brain cells in rats while they were running a maze.
keywords: while they were running a maze

answerTags.after: while they were running a maze

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: When the rats later fell asleep, the same pattern of activity was repeated, as if the animals were replaying the route in their sleep, only much faster.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So what about the other main stage of sleep, REM sleep, when most dreaming happens?

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The evidence here is less clear. However, several studies suggest REM sleep is particularly important for emotional memories, helping us keep the content of an event while reducing its painful feelings.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: There's also evidence that REM sleep helps with creative thinking, and in particular with problem solving. People who slept were far more likely to discover a hidden rule in a number puzzle than those who didn't.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Now, an intriguing question is whether we can actually strengthen memories while someone is asleep.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: In one well-known experiment in Germany, participants learned the positions of pairs of cards while a smell, the scent of roses, was present in the room.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Some participants were then exposed to the same smell during slow-wave sleep. The next day, they remembered the card positions significantly better than the others.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Researchers have tried the same thing with sounds, with similar though smaller effects.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: What about daytime naps? Many people think a nap must be at least an hour to be useful. In fact, a nap of as little as twenty minutes can improve recall.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Longer naps can bring greater benefits, but they also carry the risk of waking up from deep sleep and feeling groggy for a while.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Let's turn briefly to age. As we get older, we get less deep sleep. This may partly explain why older adults often find it harder to learn new names.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: It's not the whole story, of course, but it's an important factor, and some researchers are now testing ways of boosting deep sleep in older people.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Finally, a word for students, since many of you will have exams soon. Staying up all night before an exam is a very bad idea.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: One study found that missing a night's sleep reduced the ability to form new memories by up to 40 percent.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So my advice is simple. Rather than relying on extra hours of study late at night, go to bed at a regular time, and let your brain do some of the work for you.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Next week we'll look at dreams in more detail, so please read chapter seven before then.

passages.title: The Return of the Urban Beekeeper

paragraphs.text: Twenty years ago, keeping bees in a city was considered eccentric, the kind of pastime pursued by a handful of enthusiasts with more patience than neighbours. Today, hives sit on the roofs of hotels, offices and schools in cities from London to Tokyo, and urban honey has become a small but profitable industry. Bees were first kept on London rooftops in noticeable numbers in the 1990s, but the number of hives only rose sharply after 2008, when news reports about declining bee populations persuaded many city dwellers that they could personally help. Some companies now pay specialist firms to install and look after hives, and hand out jars of 'rooftop honey' to guests and clients as a symbol of their environmental commitment.

Supporters argue that cities offer bees a surprising advantage. Parks, gardens, cemeteries and street trees provide a variety of flowers across a long season, from early crocuses in February to late-flowering ivy in October, while pesticide use is often lower than on farmland, where huge fields may be planted with a single crop. Cities are also slightly warmer than the surrounding countryside, which allows bees to forage on cool days when rural colonies stay inside the hive. Railway embankments and canal banks, often left undisturbed for years, add further strips of wild vegetation. Many beekeepers also report that urban colonies are calmer and easier to manage, although there is little scientific evidence to support this claim.

Yet some ecologists are cautious. They point out that honeybees compete with wild pollinators for the same flowers, and that a rapid rise in hives may harm local bumblebee populations. A single honeybee colony can contain up to 50,000 workers, which together visit millions of flowers in a season, whereas a bumblebee nest rarely holds more than a few hundred insects. Productivity is also lower than many assume: a survey of 400 London hives found that city colonies yielded, on average, slightly less honey than those in the countryside, largely because forage runs out by late summer. In the most crowded districts, researchers estimated that there were more hives than the available flowers could support. Some scientists also worry that dense clusters of hives make it easier for parasites such as the varroa mite to pass from one colony to the next.

In response, several cities have introduced rules for new beekeepers. In Paris and Toronto, hives must now be registered with the local council, and some London boroughs limit the number of colonies allowed on a single building. Beginners are increasingly required to complete a short training course before they are given a permit. Supporters of the rules say that they protect not only wild insects but also the bees themselves, since poorly managed colonies are more likely to spread disease to neighbouring hives. Critics, however, argue that registration is difficult to enforce, as many hobbyists simply ignore it and inspectors rarely have time to climb onto roofs.

Other groups are focusing on food rather than hives. Community projects encourage residents to plant lavender, clover and fruit trees on balconies and in empty lots, so that both honeybees and wild species have enough to eat. One Berlin scheme has planted more than 30,000 flowering shrubs since 2015, choosing species that bloom in late summer, when food is scarcest. In London, volunteers now record the flowering times of street trees so that gaps in the food supply can be identified and filled. Some local authorities have also stopped cutting the grass on roadside verges so often, allowing wild flowers such as dandelions and knapweed to grow. Early results suggest that these 'pollinator corridors' benefit a far wider range of insects than new hives do, including butterflies, hoverflies and solitary bees.

For most urban beekeepers, profit is not the main motivation. Surveys suggest that the majority keep bees to reconnect with nature, and many donate their honey to local schools. Teachers who host hives say that pupils who were once afraid of insects quickly become fascinated by the organised life of the colony, and some schools now use the hive to teach biology, mathematics and even business skills. As one keeper put it, the real product of a city hive is not honey but curiosity. Whether that curiosity eventually extends to the thousands of less visible species that share the city with honeybees may decide whether the urban beekeeping boom is remembered as a success.

passages.title: Messages Under the Pavement: The Pneumatic Post

paragraphs.text: For roughly a century, the fastest way to send a written message across many European cities was neither the telegraph nor the telephone, but a network of metal tubes buried beneath the streets. Letters were rolled up, sealed inside cylindrical canisters and pushed through the pipes by compressed air, arriving at a distant post office within minutes. At its peak, the Paris system alone contained more than 400 kilometres of tubing, and the pale blue letter cards it carried became so familiar that Parisians simply called them 'blues'. Yet by the late twentieth century almost all of these networks had fallen silent, and today few city residents know that they ever existed.

The idea of moving objects through tubes using air pressure was not new. Engineers had experimented with it since the early nineteenth century, and several ambitious schemes proposed carrying passengers in pneumatic trains. Most of these failed, largely because it proved impossible to keep the long leather seals along the track airtight, particularly in cold or wet weather. Message tubes, by contrast, were narrow enough to be made from ordinary iron pipe, and the canisters inside them were light enough to be moved with modest amounts of pressure. The first practical system was installed in London in 1853, linking the stock exchange with the central telegraph station a few hundred metres away.

That first line reveals the problem the technology was designed to solve. The electric telegraph could carry a message between cities in seconds, but once it reached a central office it still had to be delivered by hand across congested streets. Telegraph companies found that this final stage often took longer than the transmission itself. Messenger boys on foot and horse-drawn carriages were slow and expensive, and in the busiest financial districts, where a delay of ten minutes could cost a trader a fortune, customers were unwilling to wait. Tubes offered a way to move paper between offices without entering the traffic at all.

Over the following decades, systems spread to Berlin, Vienna, Paris, Prague and dozens of other cities. Their layout varied, but most were built as a series of loops, with canisters travelling in one direction only and being transferred by hand at junction offices. Steam engines at central stations compressed air to push the carriers forward, while vacuum pumps drew them along return lines. A typical canister moved at 30 to 40 kilometres per hour, which was slower than a train but considerably faster than any vehicle in the crowded streets above. Crucially, the service was also opened to the general public, who could pay a premium to send a letter across the city in under two hours.

For ordinary citizens, the pneumatic post occupied a position somewhere between a letter and a telephone call. Diaries and novels of the period suggest that it was used for arrangements that were urgent but not quite urgent enough to justify a telegram: confirming dinner invitations, cancelling appointments or sending a quick apology. Because the letter cards were cheap and could be written in a hurry, they encouraged a brief, almost conversational style of writing. Some historians have compared this to the text messages of the early twenty-first century, although others think the comparison exaggerates how frequently most people used the service.

The decline of the tubes was gradual rather than sudden. The spread of the private telephone after the Second World War removed much of the demand for fast short messages, and the cost of maintaining ageing pipes under constantly redeveloped streets rose steadily. Blockages were a persistent difficulty: when a canister became stuck, workers had to calculate its position by measuring the air pressure, then dig up the road to remove it. Berlin closed its public network in the 1970s, and Paris followed in 1984. In most cities, the pipes were simply abandoned where they lay, and many remain underground to this day.

Yet the underlying technology never entirely disappeared. Hospitals, banks and supermarkets continue to use smaller pneumatic systems to transport blood samples, cash and documents between departments, and modern versions are controlled by computers that can route a carrier automatically to any of hundreds of stations. For some engineers, the old city networks also offer an intriguing lesson. Proposals to deliver parcels through underground pipes, reducing the number of vans on city streets, are essentially a larger version of an idea that the nineteenth century had already made work. Whether such schemes can overcome the cost of digging new tunnels beneath modern cities remains to be seen.

passages.title: The Elastic Hour: How the Mind Builds Time

paragraphs.text: Few experiences are as universal, or as puzzling, as the sense that time does not pass at a constant rate. A ten-minute wait for a delayed train can feel interminable, while an absorbing conversation of the same length seems to vanish. Older adults commonly report that the years now slip by far more quickly than they did in childhood. For much of the twentieth century, psychologists tended to explain such impressions by appealing to a single internal clock: a hypothetical pacemaker emitting regular pulses, which the brain counted in order to estimate duration. When the clock ran fast, as it was thought to do under stress or excitement, more pulses accumulated and an interval seemed longer.

The internal-clock model has proved remarkably durable, not least because it makes clear predictions that can be tested in the laboratory. Participants who are mildly warmed, given stimulants or shown threatening images do tend to overestimate short intervals, which is consistent with a pacemaker that has been sped up. Yet a growing body of research suggests that the model, at least in its simplest form, cannot account for many of the distortions people experience in everyday life. There is, for one thing, no convincing anatomical evidence of a dedicated timing organ; instead, timing-related activity appears across numerous brain regions and seems to depend heavily on the kind of task being performed.

A crucial distinction, now widely accepted, is between prospective and retrospective judgements of time. In a prospective judgement, a person knows in advance that they will be asked how long something lasts and can deliberately attend to its passage. In a retrospective judgement, the question comes as a surprise, and the person must reconstruct the duration afterwards from memory. The two appear to rely on quite different processes. Prospective estimates are strongly affected by attention: the more closely one monitors time, the more slowly it seems to pass, which is why a watched pot proverbially never boils. Retrospective estimates, by contrast, seem to be governed less by attention than by the quantity of distinct memories an interval has left behind.

This distinction helps to resolve what is sometimes called the holiday paradox. While on an unfamiliar and eventful holiday, people often feel that the days are flying past, since their attention is occupied by novel surroundings rather than by the clock. On returning home, however, the same week may seem to have lasted far longer than a week at work, because it is richly stocked with separate memories. A routine week, which may have dragged at the time, collapses in retrospect into a handful of indistinguishable recollections. The paradox, in other words, arises because experience and memory apply different measures to the same stretch of time.

Laboratory studies of the so-called oddball effect point in a similar direction. When participants watch a sequence of identical images interrupted by a single unexpected one, they consistently judge the unexpected image to have been displayed for longer, even when all the images appeared for exactly the same period. One interpretation is that the brain responds less vigorously to stimuli it has already encountered and can predict, and that this reduced response is misread as a shorter duration. On this account, the perception of time is not read directly from a clock at all but inferred from the amount of neural effort that a moment demands.

Such findings have prompted a reinterpretation of the familiar complaint that life accelerates with age. Although the complaint has sometimes been attributed to a general slowing of biological processes, there is little experimental support for the idea that older people's judgements of short intervals differ markedly from those of younger adults. A more persuasive explanation may be that adult life simply contains fewer genuinely new experiences. Childhood and adolescence are crowded with first occasions, such as first journeys, first jobs and first friendships, each of which lays down a distinct memory. Later decades, organised around established routines, may provide memory with less material from which to reconstruct their length.

If this reasoning is correct, it carries a modestly encouraging implication. The apparent speed of passing years may not be an inevitable consequence of ageing but, at least in part, a product of how one lives. Some researchers have suggested, only half in jest, that deliberately seeking out novelty, whether by learning a skill, visiting unfamiliar places or varying daily routes, might lengthen one's life, not in objective terms but in the way it is remembered. The claim remains largely untested, and critics caution that novelty can itself become routine. Nevertheless, it reflects a significant shift in thinking: time, as experienced, is less something the mind measures than something it constructs.

passages.title: School Streets: Reclaiming the Road at the School Gate

paragraphs.text: Every weekday morning, the roads around many primary schools follow the same pattern. For about twenty minutes, cars queue along narrow streets, park on pavements and turn in tight spaces while children and parents try to squeeze past them. Once the bell rings, the traffic disappears as quickly as it arrived. For decades this daily rush was accepted as an unavoidable part of school life. In recent years, however, a simple idea has begun to change it: closing the street outside the school gate to motor traffic at the start and end of the school day.

These 'school streets', as they are usually known, work in a straightforward way. Signs are placed at each end of the road, and for a fixed period, often from 8.15 to 9.15 in the morning and from 2.45 to 3.45 in the afternoon, only pedestrians and cyclists may enter. Residents who live on the street, as well as emergency vehicles and drivers with disabilities, are normally allowed through. In some places, the closure is enforced by volunteers who move temporary barriers into position; in others, cameras record the number plates of vehicles that enter without permission, and drivers receive a fine by post.

The first schemes appeared in northern Italy in the late 1980s, but the idea spread slowly at first. It gained momentum in the 2010s, when concern about air pollution near schools grew rapidly. Studies had shown that children are particularly vulnerable to traffic fumes, partly because they breathe faster than adults and partly because their height places them closer to vehicle exhausts. By 2020, several hundred schemes were operating in Britain alone, and the number rose sharply during the coronavirus pandemic, when local authorities were given emergency funding to create more space for walking and cycling.

Evidence about the effects of school streets is still being collected, but early results are encouraging. One evaluation of thirty-seven schemes in a large English city found that levels of nitrogen dioxide, a gas produced mainly by diesel engines, fell by up to 23 per cent outside participating schools during the morning closure. Over the same period, the proportion of children who walked, cycled or scooted to school rose, while the number who were driven fell by around a fifth. Head teachers also reported that the atmosphere at the school gate had changed, with parents stopping to talk rather than hurrying back to their cars, and a large majority of parents said they would like the scheme to continue.

Not everyone is convinced. One common concern is that traffic is simply moved onto neighbouring roads, where parents park instead. Monitoring suggests that this happens in some cases, although the extra traffic on surrounding streets is usually smaller than feared, because some families change their habits altogether rather than parking a little further away. Other objections come from residents who, although allowed to drive through, must explain themselves to volunteers every day, and from parents who drive their children to school on the way to work and see the closures as an unfair burden.

Planners emphasise that the success of a scheme depends heavily on local conditions. School streets work best on short, quiet roads with no through traffic, where a closure causes little disruption; they are much harder to introduce outside schools on main roads or bus routes. Involving the community early also appears to matter. In one town, a trial that was introduced with little warning was abandoned after a month of complaints, while a similar scheme nearby, designed after meetings with parents, residents and pupils, is still in place six years later.

For some supporters, the real importance of school streets lies beyond the school gate. By showing that a street can be used for something other than moving and parking cars, even for just two hours a day, the schemes invite residents to imagine other possibilities. In several cities, closures that began as school streets have become permanent pedestrian areas, complete with benches, planters and play equipment. Children who once had to hold an adult's hand on the pavement can now chalk pictures on the road. What started as a response to a morning traffic jam may yet change how communities think about the space outside their front doors.

passages.title: Chrononutrition: Does the Clock on the Plate Matter?

paragraphs.text: Nutrition advice has traditionally focused on two questions: what we eat, and how much. A third question, when we eat, has until recently received far less attention. Over the past two decades, however, a field known as chrononutrition has begun to examine whether the timing of meals affects health independently of their content. Its central claim is that the body processes identical food differently depending on the hour at which it arrives, and that eating out of step with our internal rhythms may contribute to weight gain and metabolic disease.

The idea rests on the discovery that almost every tissue in the body contains its own biological clock. A master clock in the brain, set largely by exposure to daylight, coordinates the activity of these peripheral clocks, which regulate processes such as the release of digestive enzymes and the sensitivity of cells to insulin, the hormone that controls blood sugar. Crucially, the peripheral clocks in the liver and gut are influenced not only by light but also by food. When meals arrive at unusual times, these clocks can drift out of alignment with the master clock, a condition researchers describe as internal desynchrony.

Some of the strongest evidence comes from studies of shift workers, who regularly eat and sleep at times that conflict with daylight. Large surveys have found that people with long histories of night work have higher rates of type 2 diabetes and obesity than day workers, even after differences in diet and physical activity are taken into account. Such observational studies cannot prove cause and effect, since night workers may differ from day workers in other ways. Controlled laboratory experiments, however, have produced similar findings. When healthy volunteers were kept on a schedule in which they ate and slept twelve hours out of phase with their normal routine, their blood sugar after meals rose within days to levels usually seen in people at risk of diabetes.

Laboratory work has also shown that the same meal produces a noticeably larger rise in blood sugar when eaten in the evening than in the morning. This appears to be because insulin sensitivity is highest early in the day and declines as evening approaches. In one trial, two groups of overweight adults followed diets containing identical numbers of calories for twelve weeks. The group that consumed most of its daily energy at breakfast lost significantly more weight than the group that ate its largest meal in the evening. Findings like these have given new life to the old saying that one should breakfast like a king and dine like a pauper.

A related approach, known as time-restricted eating, limits all food intake to a window of eight to ten hours each day, without necessarily changing what or how much is eaten. Experiments in mice produced striking results: animals fed a high-fat diet within a restricted window remained considerably leaner than those given the same food around the clock. Human trials have been more modest. Some have reported improvements in blood pressure and insulin sensitivity, but others have found that participants lose weight mainly because a shorter eating window leads them, without intending to, to eat less.

It is here that the enthusiasm surrounding chrononutrition deserves some caution. Many of the human studies involve small numbers of participants followed for only a few weeks, and the results of different trials do not always agree. Individual variation also complicates the picture. People differ in their chronotype, their natural tendency to be active early or late in the day, and a schedule that suits a so-called morning lark may not suit a night owl. There is also a practical difficulty: family routines, working hours and social life often make an early evening meal impossible, and advice that people cannot follow is of limited value.

Nonetheless, most researchers in the field agree on a few cautious recommendations. Eating a substantial breakfast, avoiding large meals late at night and keeping mealtimes reasonably regular from day to day are unlikely to cause harm and may bring benefits, particularly for people at risk of metabolic disease. What chrononutrition does not yet justify is the confident, one-size-fits-all rules promoted by some diet books, which often present early findings from small studies as settled fact. The clock, it seems, is one ingredient in a healthy diet, but it is not a substitute for the others.

passages.title: The Shop That Came to the Door

paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, households in the remote villages of northern England and Scotland did a large part of their shopping without ever leaving home. Twice a week, sometimes more, a converted lorry or van would pull up at the end of the lane, a bell would ring, and residents would climb aboard to buy bread, paraffin, tinned goods and sewing thread. These mobile shops, known locally as 'travellers', filled a gap that fixed retailers could not afford to serve. At their peak in the late 1950s, one trade directory listed more than 2,300 of them operating across Britain. For many families, the arrival of the van was one of the fixed points of the week.

The earliest mobile shops were horse-drawn carts, often run by bakers or grocers who wanted to reach customers beyond walking distance of their premises. The real expansion, however, came after the First World War, when thousands of ex-army lorries were sold off cheaply. Enterprising shopkeepers fitted these vehicles with wooden shelves, a counter at the rear and, in some cases, a small paraffin stove to keep the driver warm in winter. By 1930 a well-equipped van could carry around 400 different items, a range that would have impressed many village shops of the time. Some firms painted their vans in bright colours and gave them names, partly so that customers could recognise them from a distance across open fields.

Running a traveller was demanding work. A typical owner-driver started before dawn, loading stock from a wholesaler in the nearest market town, and might not return until after dark. Routes were planned with great care: each village had to be visited on the same day and at roughly the same time every week, because customers organised their household routines around the van's arrival. Records kept by one Cumbrian operator, Walter Heslop, show that he covered 190 miles a week and served about 340 regular households. His ledgers also reveal that almost a third of his sales were made on credit, with families settling their accounts at the end of each month.

The mobile shop was more than a place to buy goods. For elderly or isolated residents, the weekly visit was frequently their main contact with the outside world. Drivers delivered letters, passed on news from neighbouring farms and occasionally collected prescriptions from the chemist in town. Oral history interviews recorded in the 1990s suggest that many former customers remembered the driver's conversation as clearly as the goods they bought. Some operators even acted as informal bankers, cashing cheques for pensioners who lived many miles from the nearest branch.

From the 1960s onwards, however, the trade entered a long decline. Rising car ownership meant that more rural families could drive to supermarkets, where prices were lower and choice was far greater. At the same time, stricter food hygiene regulations required operators to install refrigeration and running water, investments that many small businesses could not justify. The number of mobile shops fell steadily, and by 1985 fewer than 400 were thought to remain in operation. In some areas the closure of village schools and post offices also reduced the number of people living in remote settlements, shrinking the customer base still further. Operators who survived often did so by specialising, for example in fresh fish or hardware, rather than trying to compete with supermarkets on price.

Recently, though, the idea has begun to return in a new form. Several rural councils have supported community-owned vans that combine a small grocery with services such as parcel collection and library loans. Unlike their predecessors, these vehicles use card readers and online ordering, allowing customers to request specific products in advance. Supporters argue that they reduce the number of individual car journeys and help older residents remain independent. Critics, on the other hand, point out that most of these schemes still depend on public grants and have yet to show that they can survive on sales alone.

Whether the modern traveller will become a permanent feature of rural life remains uncertain. What is clear is that the original mobile shops solved a problem that has never entirely disappeared: how to bring everyday goods to people who live far from the places where those goods are sold. Historians of retailing have begun to take a closer interest in the subject, and a small collection of restored vans can now be seen at a transport museum in County Durham, where visitors are invited to step inside and imagine the busy Saturday rounds of the past.

paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, the accepted wisdom in language teaching was that the classroom should be a monolingual space. Pupils learning English, French or Spanish were expected to hear and use only the target language, and teachers who slipped into the pupils' home language were often regarded as having failed. The reasoning seemed straightforward: the more exposure learners received to the new language, the faster they would acquire it, and every minute spent in their first language was a minute lost. Textbooks of the period frequently included advice on how to avoid translation altogether, recommending gestures, pictures and demonstrations instead.

Over the past two decades, this assumption has been challenged by a growing body of classroom research. Linguists working in multilingual schools noticed that pupils routinely moved between languages when discussing difficult ideas with one another, even when teachers had banned the practice. Rather than treating this behaviour as a sign of weakness, some researchers began to describe it as a resource. The term 'translanguaging', originally used to describe a bilingual teaching method in Welsh schools, came to refer more broadly to the ways in which multilingual speakers draw on their full range of languages in order to make meaning.

One of the more detailed investigations was carried out over three years in eleven secondary schools in a large port city, where more than forty home languages were spoken. The research team, led by the applied linguist Dr Maren Oduya, compared science lessons in which pupils were permitted to discuss new concepts in any language with lessons conducted strictly in English. Pupils in the flexible classes scored, on average, 12 per cent higher on end-of-unit tests. Perhaps more surprisingly, their written English was no weaker than that of the control group, and in some cases their use of technical vocabulary was more precise.

Oduya's team suggested that the explanation lay in the difference between understanding a concept and expressing it. When pupils first met a complex idea, such as the distinction between mass and weight, they were able to work out its meaning through discussion in the language they knew best. Once the concept was secure, attaching the English terms to it became a relatively simple task. In the English-only lessons, by contrast, many pupils appeared to memorise the vocabulary without fully grasping the idea behind it, and this weakness became evident when they were asked to apply the concept to an unfamiliar problem. Several teachers in the study also reported that pupils who had worked through a concept in their home language asked more questions in the later, English-medium part of the lesson.

Not everyone is persuaded. Critics argue that the benefits reported in such studies may depend heavily on the skill of individual teachers, and that in less carefully managed classrooms the home language can easily come to dominate. There is also a practical difficulty: in a class where pupils speak a dozen different languages, the teacher cannot possibly understand every conversation, and may therefore be unable to identify misunderstandings. A small-scale study in a rural district found that, without clear rules about when each language should be used, pupils' exposure to English fell by almost half within a single term. Some teachers also worry that pupils who share a home language may unintentionally exclude classmates who do not speak it.

Supporters of translanguaging accept that it is not a method that can simply be switched on. They stress that it works best as a planned strategy rather than an informal tolerance of mixed language use. In the classrooms observed by Oduya's team, teachers typically allowed open discussion in any language during the early stages of a task, but required the final written product to be in English. Some schools also produced bilingual glossaries, compiled partly by the pupils themselves, which linked key terms in English to their equivalents in the most widely spoken home languages.

The debate has implications that go beyond language teaching. If pupils' home languages are treated as a tool for learning rather than an obstacle, schools may need to reconsider how they train teachers, design assessments and communicate with parents. For many families, the change of attitude also carries a symbolic value. Parents interviewed during the port city study frequently said that their children had become less reluctant to use the family language at home once it had been welcomed at school, a result that the researchers had not set out to measure but considered among the most significant of the project. Whether such effects can be reproduced in other settings is a question that further research will need to address.
