paragraphs.text: When a person asks a company to delete their personal data, the request is, in principle, simple to satisfy: the relevant records are located and erased. For organisations that use machine learning, however, the situation is considerably more complicated. A model trained on millions of examples does not store those examples in a form that can be neatly removed; instead, the information is dispersed across billions of numerical parameters, each shaped slightly by every piece of data the model encountered. Deleting the original record from a database leaves the model's learned behaviour untouched, and in some cases the model may still be able to reproduce fragments of the data it was trained on.

This mismatch has given rise to a field known as machine unlearning, which seeks methods for removing the influence of specific data from a trained model. The most reliable approach is also the most obvious: discard the model and retrain it from scratch without the offending data. For small systems this is practical, but for large models the cost is prohibitive. One estimate, produced by an industry consortium, put the energy required to retrain a single large language model at roughly the annual electricity consumption of 1,200 households, a figure that makes routine retraining in response to individual requests unrealistic.

Researchers have therefore explored cheaper alternatives. One early proposal, sometimes described as 'sharded' training, involves dividing the training data into many separate portions and training a smaller sub-model on each. When a deletion request arrives, only the sub-model that saw the relevant data needs to be retrained. The approach reduces costs substantially, but it has a drawback: models assembled from many independently trained parts tend to perform less well than a single model trained on all the data at once, and the loss of accuracy grows as the number of shards increases. Choosing how many shards to use therefore involves a trade-off between the cost of future deletions and the quality of the model.

A second family of techniques attempts to reverse the effect of particular examples directly, by adjusting the model's parameters in the opposite direction to the changes those examples originally caused. These 'approximate' methods are fast, often requiring only minutes of computation, but they raise a difficult question of verification. Because a model's behaviour emerges from the interaction of vast numbers of parameters, it is hard to demonstrate that the influence of a particular record has genuinely disappeared rather than merely become less visible. In one series of experiments, a team of researchers found that models which appeared to have forgotten certain training examples could be prompted to recall them after a small amount of further training on unrelated material.

The verification problem is not merely technical; it also has legal and ethical dimensions. Data protection laws in several jurisdictions grant individuals a right to have their information erased, but these laws were drafted with conventional databases in mind and say little about statistical models. Regulators have so far been reluctant to state whether an approximately unlearned model satisfies an erasure request. Some legal scholars argue that the law should require only that the model no longer reveals the individual's data; others maintain that any residual influence, however small, amounts to continued processing of personal information. Until the question is settled, companies face considerable uncertainty about what they must do when a request arrives.

There is also a broader concern about who benefits from unlearning. The techniques were initially discussed as a means of protecting privacy, but the same methods could be used to remove material for less admirable reasons: to conceal evidence of biased training data, for instance, or to erase content that a company later finds commercially inconvenient. Because unlearning leaves few visible traces, outsiders may have no way of knowing what has been removed. For this reason, several researchers have proposed that any use of unlearning should be recorded in an independent log, open to inspection by auditors, though no such system yet exists on a large scale.

It seems unlikely that a single solution will emerge. What the debate has already achieved, however, is a shift in how developers think about data at the design stage. Rather than treating training data as a permanent foundation, some organisations now keep detailed records of which data was used to train which model, and structure their systems so that particular sources can be withdrawn later if necessary. In this sense, the ability to forget is gradually becoming part of how machine learning systems are built, rather than a repair attempted after the fact.

passages.title: Echoes in Stone: The Science of Archaeoacoustics

paragraphs.text: Archaeologists have traditionally reconstructed the past through what can be seen and handled: walls, pottery, tools, bones. Sound, by its nature, leaves no direct physical trace, and for most of the discipline's history it was assumed to lie beyond the reach of scientific study. Over the past thirty years, however, a small but increasingly influential group of researchers has argued that the acoustic properties of ancient spaces can be measured, modelled and interpreted, and that doing so may reveal aspects of past experience that conventional methods overlook. The field they have created is known as archaeoacoustics.

The basic techniques are borrowed from architectural acoustics. Researchers place a sound source, typically a loudspeaker emitting a sweeping tone or a sharp burst of noise, at a chosen point within a structure and record the result with microphones positioned elsewhere. From these recordings they calculate measures such as reverberation time, the period taken for a sound to fade by sixty decibels, and identify resonant frequencies at which the space amplifies sound. Where a structure has been partly destroyed, digital models can be used to estimate how it would originally have sounded, although the reliability of such reconstructions depends heavily on assumptions about missing roofs, wall coverings and the number of people present. Measurements are usually repeated several times at each position, and at different times of day, to reduce the influence of wind and background noise.

Some of the most striking results have come from underground chambers. In surveys of a group of Neolithic rock-cut tombs on a Mediterranean island, researchers found that several inner chambers resonated strongly at frequencies between 95 and 120 hertz, a range that falls within the lower register of the adult male voice. Chanting at these frequencies produced a powerful, almost physical sensation that participants described as seeming to come from the walls themselves. Similar resonances have since been reported at sites in Ireland and Peru, prompting speculation that ancient builders may have deliberately shaped spaces to enhance vocal performance.

It is this last claim that has attracted the sharpest criticism. Sceptics point out that almost any enclosed stone chamber of a certain size will resonate within the range of the human voice, simply as a consequence of its dimensions. Demonstrating that a resonance exists is therefore very different from demonstrating that it was intended. In a widely discussed review, the acoustician Tomas Revel argued that many early archaeoacoustic studies had examined only sites where interesting effects were expected, and had rarely compared them with ordinary structures of similar shape. Without such comparisons, he noted, researchers risked mistaking accidental properties for evidence of design. Revel did not reject the field as a whole, however; he argued that its methods needed to become more rigorous if its conclusions were to be taken seriously.

Partly in response to these objections, more recent projects have adopted a comparative approach. A study of prehistoric rock art in a river valley in southern Africa measured echo strength at 64 painted rock shelters and at 58 unpainted shelters nearby. Painted locations were found to produce noticeably stronger echoes on average, a pattern that would be difficult to explain by chance. The researchers were careful, however, not to conclude that the paintings were placed for acoustic reasons alone; they suggested instead that sound may have been one of several factors, alongside visibility and access to water, that made certain locations seem significant.

Archaeoacoustics also raises questions about how evidence of experience should be interpreted. Even if a resonance was deliberately created, we cannot know with confidence how it was perceived. A sensation that a modern visitor finds uncanny may have been ordinary to people who encountered it regularly, and the meanings attached to sound vary enormously between cultures. Written records, where they exist, rarely describe sound in any detail, which makes the task harder still. For this reason, some practitioners have begun to work alongside anthropologists who study present-day communities, not to project modern beliefs onto the past, but to widen the range of possible interpretations that archaeologists consider.

Despite these uncertainties, the field has had a noticeable effect on museum and heritage practice. Several sites now offer visitors recordings or live demonstrations designed to convey how a space would once have sounded, and conservation plans increasingly include acoustic measurements taken before any restoration work begins, since the addition of modern flooring or lighting can subtly alter a chamber's acoustic character. Whether or not the grander claims about intentional design are eventually confirmed, archaeoacoustics has at least ensured that the sensory dimension of ancient places is no longer ignored.

task1.prompt: The graph shows the percentage of households with internet access in three countries between 2000 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features.

modelAnswer.text:
The line graph compares the proportion of households with internet access in Canada, Brazil and India between 2000 and 2020.

Overall, access rose steadily in all three countries over the period, although Canada remained the most connected nation throughout, while India, despite starting from the lowest base, recorded the most dramatic growth in the final decade.

In 2000, just over two-fifths of Canadian households (42%) were online, compared with 18% in Brazil and a mere 9% in India. Over the following ten years, the Canadian figure climbed to 66%, whereas Brazil saw its share more than double to 47%. India, by contrast, progressed relatively slowly, reaching only 24% by 2010.

From 2010 onwards, the gap between the three countries narrowed considerably. Canada continued its upward trend to finish at 82% in 2020, and Brazil rose at a similar pace to 72%. Meanwhile, the proportion of connected homes in India accelerated sharply, more than doubling in ten years to reach 55% by the end of the period, although it still lagged some way behind the other two countries.

task1.title: International tourist arrivals in three cities
task1.prompt: The graph below shows the number of international tourists (in millions) who visited three cities between 2004 and 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The line graph illustrates how many international visitors, in millions, travelled to Lisbon, Prague and Vienna over a twenty-year period from 2004 to 2024.

Overall, all three cities attracted more foreign tourists by the end of the period, despite a dramatic collapse in 2020. The most striking feature is the rapid rise of Lisbon, which began as the least visited city but finished well ahead of the other two.

In 2004, Prague was the most popular destination with 4.2 million arrivals, followed by Vienna with 3.5 million, while Lisbon received only 2.1 million. Over the next twelve years, Prague and Vienna grew steadily, reaching 5.6 and 4.7 million respectively in 2016. Over the past decade, remote work has shifted from a rare privilege to a mainstream arrangement for millions of office staff. In my view, its advantages for both employers and employees clearly outweigh the drawbacks, provided that it is managed sensibly.

As a result, workers who are trusted to manage their own schedules are often more loyal and less likely to resign.

Admittedly, working from home is not without its challenges. Some staff feel isolated, and junior employees may miss the informal learning that happens in a shared office. However, these problems can largely be solved through regular video meetings and occasional in-person days rather than by abandoning remote work altogether. As a result, some fall into debt soon after receiving their first salary, while others rely heavily on processed food. Moreover, not every child grows up in a household where these lessons are passed on, so the school may be the only place where disadvantaged pupils can acquire them.

On the other hand, academic subjects provide the foundation for almost everything else. A student cannot understand interest rates without mathematics, nor read a rental contract carefully without strong literacy. Furthermore, subjects such as science and history develop analytical thinking, which is essential for higher education and for many careers. If these were reduced significantly, school leavers might be able to cook but would be poorly equipped to compete in a knowledge-based economy.

In my view, the most sensible solution is to combine the two. Mathematics lessons, for instance, could include projects on household budgeting, and science classes could explore nutrition through practical cookery. A second cause is inadequate waste management. Several measures could reduce this pollution. Governments should impose taxes on, or ban, the most common single-use items. Secondly, wealthier nations and international organisations could fund better waste collection and recycling facilities in regions where rubbish currently escapes into waterways. In addition, deposit-return schemes, in which customers receive a small refund for returning bottles, have proved highly effective at increasing recycling rates. In many countries, more and more people are choosing to live alone. What are the reasons for this? Do you think it is a positive or negative development?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

for: Reason: people marry later or not at all
Reason: greater financial independence, especially among women
Positive: privacy and personal freedom
Positive: develops independence and self-reliance
against: Reason: longer life expectancy leaves many elderly people widowed
Negative: loneliness and mental health problems
Negative: higher housing demand and costs
Negative: less efficient use of energy and space

modelAnswer.text:
The number of single-person households has risen sharply in many countries over recent decades. In this essay, I will explore why this has happened and explain why I consider it a mixed, but mainly negative, development.

One key reason is that people are marrying later, or choosing not to marry at all, so there is a longer period of adulthood spent outside a family home. Rising incomes, particularly among women, have also made it financially possible for many adults to rent or buy a home of their own. In addition, because people now live longer, many elderly people continue to live alone after the death of a partner, often for twenty years or more.

Living alone certainly offers some benefits. It gives people complete privacy and control over their own space, and it can encourage independence and self-reliance. For young professionals, a period of living alone may be an important stage of personal development.

However, I believe the disadvantages are more serious. The most significant is loneliness, which research has linked to depression and poorer physical health, especially among older people who may go days without speaking to anyone. Furthermore, when each person occupies a separate flat, cities need far more housing, which pushes up prices and increases energy consumption, since heating and appliances are shared by fewer people. In already crowded cities such as London or Seoul, this places heavy pressure on the housing market.

In conclusion, the trend towards living alone results from later marriage, greater financial independence and longer lives. Although it brings freedom and privacy, its social and environmental costs lead me to view it as a largely negative development that governments and communities should take steps to address.

task2.title: Youth crime
task2.prompt:
In some countries, the number of crimes committed by teenagers is increasing. What are the causes of this, and what solutions can you suggest?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

for: Cause: lack of parental supervision
Cause: poverty and limited opportunities
Cause: peer pressure and gang culture
Cause: school exclusion and boredom
against: Solution: youth centres, sport and mentoring programmes
Solution: support for struggling families
Solution: keep at-risk pupils in education
Solution: restorative justice rather than prison for first offences

modelAnswer.text:
In a number of countries, crime committed by teenagers appears to be on the rise, causing concern among parents and policymakers alike. This essay will discuss the main causes of this problem and propose several possible solutions.

The first cause is often found within the family. When parents work long hours or are absent altogether, teenagers may receive little supervision or guidance, and they are more likely to spend unstructured time on the streets. A second factor is poverty. Young people growing up in deprived neighbourhoods may see few legitimate routes to success, and some are tempted by the quick money offered by theft or drug dealing. Peer pressure also plays an important role, since adolescents are strongly influenced by the need to belong, and joining a group that breaks the law can seem attractive to those who feel excluded at school.

To tackle these causes, a combination of measures is required. Local authorities should invest in youth centres, sports clubs and mentoring schemes that offer young people a safe place to go and positive adult role models. Schools, meanwhile, should try to keep struggling pupils in education by providing extra support rather than excluding them, as exclusion frequently leads directly to crime. In addition, social services could offer practical help to families under strain. Finally, for first-time offenders, restorative justice, in which young people meet their victims and repair the harm they have caused, has been shown to reduce reoffending more effectively than detention.

In conclusion, youth crime is closely linked to weak supervision, poverty and peer influence. By providing constructive activities, educational support and more rehabilitative forms of justice, society can prevent many teenagers from following a criminal path.

task2.title: Negative news
task2.prompt:
News media tend to focus mainly on problems and negative events rather than positive developments. Some people think this is harmful to individuals and society. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

for: Constant bad news can raise anxiety and hopelessness
Gives a distorted, overly pessimistic view of the world
May reduce trust in institutions and each other
Positive stories could inspire people to act
against: Journalism's role is to expose problems and hold power to account
Warning people about risks keeps them safe
Audiences choose to read dramatic stories
Positive news can seem like propaganda or advertising

modelAnswer.text:
It is often observed that newspapers, television and news websites concentrate heavily on disasters, crime and conflict while largely ignoring positive events. I partly agree that this has harmful effects, but I also believe that reporting problems is an essential function of the media.

There is little doubt that an unbalanced diet of bad news can damage individuals. People who follow the news closely may develop a sense of anxiety and helplessness, particularly when stories about war or climate change appear hour after hour on their phones. Moreover, constant negativity can distort people's understanding of the world. Many surveys have found that the public believes crime and poverty are increasing even in periods when they are actually falling, largely because dramatic incidents receive so much coverage. Such pessimism can undermine trust in institutions and discourage people from taking part in public life.

On the other hand, journalists are not simply entertainers. One of their most important duties is to expose corruption, injustice and danger so that governments and companies can be held accountable. A report on unsafe buildings or contaminated water may be deeply unpleasant, but it can save lives. If the media focused mainly on good news, they would risk becoming a kind of public relations service for the powerful.

The solution, in my opinion, is not to abandon negative reporting but to balance it. So-called constructive journalism, which explains what is being done to solve a problem as well as describing the problem itself, can inform audiences without leaving them feeling powerless.

In conclusion, although the media's focus on negative events can cause anxiety and a distorted view of reality, reporting problems remains vital. A more balanced approach would serve both individuals and society better.

task2.title: Multinational companies
task2.prompt:
Large multinational companies are opening branches and factories in many developing countries. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

for: Creates jobs and raises wages
Transfers technology and management skills
Brings investment and tax revenue
Improves infrastructure and access to goods
against: Local businesses may be driven out
Profits flow back to wealthy countries
Risk of poor working conditions and pollution
Loss of cultural identity and local traditions

modelAnswer.text:
Over the past few decades, multinational corporations have established offices and factories in a large number of developing nations. While this trend raises legitimate concerns, I believe that its advantages generally outweigh the disadvantages.

The most important benefit is employment. A single factory run by an international firm can provide thousands of jobs, often at wages higher than those offered by local employers. Bangladesh's garment industry and Vietnam's electronics sector, for example, have lifted millions of people out of poverty in this way. In addition, multinationals bring technology and management expertise that gradually spread to local companies, as employees gain skills and later start their own businesses. Governments also benefit from tax revenue and from improvements to roads, ports and power supplies that such investment often requires.

However, the presence of global companies is not without problems. Small local firms may be unable to compete with the prices and marketing power of international brands, and some are forced to close. Furthermore, a large share of the profits is transferred to shareholders in wealthier countries rather than reinvested locally. There have also been serious cases of unsafe working conditions and environmental damage where regulation is weak.

Nevertheless, most of these drawbacks can be reduced through sensible policy rather than by rejecting foreign investment. Developing countries can enforce labour and environmental standards, require companies to source some materials locally and invest tax revenue in education, so that their own businesses become more competitive over time.

In conclusion, although multinational companies can harm local businesses and exploit weak regulation, the jobs, skills and investment they bring are substantial. With effective government oversight, I believe the advantages of their expansion clearly outweigh the disadvantages.

task2.title: Spending on space exploration
task2.prompt:
Some people think that governments should stop spending money on space exploration and use it to solve problems on Earth instead. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

for: Poverty, hunger and healthcare need urgent funding
Climate change requires massive investment
Private companies can now fund space projects
Public money should meet citizens' immediate needs
against: Space research produces useful technologies (satellites, materials)
Satellites monitor climate and disasters
Space budgets are small compared with total spending
Exploration inspires young people to study science

modelAnswer.text:
Some argue that the vast sums spent on space programmes would be better used to tackle poverty, disease and climate change here on Earth. Although I understand this view, I disagree that governments should abandon space exploration altogether.

Those who support the proposal make a reasonable point. Millions of people still lack clean water, adequate healthcare or enough to eat, and it may seem morally difficult to justify sending rockets to Mars while these needs remain unmet. Furthermore, private companies are now willing to invest in rockets and satellites themselves, so it could be argued that taxpayers no longer need to fund this work.

However, I believe this argument overlooks several important points. Firstly, space research has produced technologies that directly improve life on Earth. Satellite systems provide weather forecasts, navigation and communications, and they allow scientists to monitor deforestation, melting ice caps and rising sea levels with great accuracy. Without them, our response to climate change and natural disasters would be far less effective. Secondly, the budgets involved are relatively modest. In most countries with space programmes, spending on space represents less than one per cent of the government budget, so cancelling it would do little to solve global poverty. Finally, space exploration inspires young people to study science and engineering, fields on which future solutions to earthly problems will depend.

It is also questionable whether private firms, which are driven by profit, should control research that affects all of humanity.

In conclusion, while problems on Earth must remain a priority, space exploration contributes to solving many of them and costs comparatively little. Governments should therefore continue to fund it, alongside, rather than instead of, their efforts to improve life on our own planet.
